**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Breed expression, Owner dynamics

**Distinguish from:** Pushy mouthing that escalates when challenged is hardship, not substitution. A Retriever holding a toy is breed expression. Licking that tracks handler anxiety is owner dynamics layered on top.

**Substitution:** Offer a mouth job — Hold, soft toy to carry — or guide Chin/Nose for calm static contact. Answer what instead of licking skin.

**Decoupling:** Never introduce a lickmat or smeared container immediately after a human-licking episode — that rewards the wrong trigger. Dedicated lick outlets only at separate scheduled times when calm.

**Proactive guidance:** Say Chin or Nose calmly; cup flat hand under jaw for one to two seconds; treat from the other hand. Nominate the preferred behaviour before suppression.

**Guide section:** [symptom compulsive lick handler](#compulsive-licking-of-handler)

##### Demanding paw on handler

Forceful repeated pawing for attention — demand loop, not affection.

**Linked patterns:** Anxious attachment, Frenetic arousal

**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Owner dynamics

**Distinguish from:** Soft anxious paw with whale eye is insecurity — substitution path. Hard pushy paw with stiff body is entitlement — hardship path.

**Substitution:** Withhold attention until calm; offer Chin or place as the script for contact.

**Decoupling:** Never treat or praise during the paw — become a rock until four on the floor.

**Proactive guidance:** Guide into Chin or down before the paw lands; reward the nominated behaviour only.

**Guide section:** [symptom demand paw handler](#demanding-paw-on-handler)

##### Demand lean at thresholds

Pressure lean at doors or gates — demand for access, distinct from trust lean at rest.

**Linked patterns:** Anxious attachment, Barrier frustration

**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Skill gap — never taught

**Distinguish from:** Trust lean at rest in living mode is different from threshold pressure in training mode — see context of contact.

**Substitution:** Wait or place at threshold; earned access through calm accountability.

**Decoupling:** Do not open the door while the dog leans — release only on calm default.

**Proactive guidance:** Front door protocol — nominate sit or wait before handle turns.

**Guide section:** [symptom demand lean threshold](#demand-lean-at-thresholds)

##### Velcro following indoors

Cannot break contact with handler when moving room to room — anxious attachment, not separation.

**Linked patterns:** Anxious attachment, Handler-sensitive

**Confusable drivers:** Breed expression, Owner dynamics

**Distinguish from:** Clingy breed bonding is context — velcro that panics when blocked needs structure plus substitution, not unlimited lap access.

**Substitution:** Place or bed at distance; mouth job during transitions; earned access to follow.

**Decoupling:** Do not reward shadowing with constant talk and touch — neutral movement, reward check-ins.

**Proactive guidance:** Short separations with wins; build independence through access training.

**Guide section:** [symptom velcro follow handler](#velcro-following-indoors)

##### Whale eye when handler looms

Whites visible, head turned — extreme anxiety, not sass or guilt.

**Linked patterns:** Handler-sensitive, Fear reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Social dominance (dog-dog)

**Distinguish from:** Not dominance — do not confront stare-for-stare. Not guilt — create space.

**Substitution:** Lower loom; approach from side; Chin or calm contact when dog initiates.

**Decoupling:** Do not force interaction or scold — confirms unsafe world.

**Proactive guidance:** Ready stance without anxious watching; peripheral awareness.

**Guide section:** [symptom whale eye handler](#whale-eye-when-handler-looms)

##### Submissive urination on greeting

Deference puddle under pressure — greeting, loom, or sharp voice.

**Linked patterns:** Fear reactive, Handler-sensitive

**Confusable drivers:** Age & development, Trauma & security-first

**Distinguish from:** Young or traumatised dogs — not spite. Lower energy, not firmer correction.

**Substitution:** Greet low and side-on; no overhead reach; small wins rebuilding confidence.

**Decoupling:** Do not react dramatically to the puddle — neutral cleanup, lower threshold next time.

**Proactive guidance:** Outdoor greeting first; build trust before indoor excitement.

**Guide section:** [symptom submissive urination greeting](#submissive-urination-on-greeting)

##### Freeze-and-tolerate under handling

Goes still and endures petting or handling like a stuffed animal — learned helplessness from ignored boundaries, not calm enjoyment.

**Linked patterns:** Handler-sensitive, Fear reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Owner dynamics, Trauma & security-first

**Distinguish from:** A genuinely relaxed dog is loose and soft and re-initiates contact. Still-but-stiff, tense, or lip-licking while tolerating is shutdown — cortisol high, signals given up. Not stubbornness.

**Substitution:** Run the consent test — one to two hands for five seconds, then stop and read re-initiation. Reduce handling volume; let the dog opt in.

**Decoupling:** Do not reward tolerating by continuing or escalating touch. Never smother a dog that has gone still — stillness is not consent.

**Proactive guidance:** Three-second pause before touch; reach for chest not skull; stop the moment the body stiffens or the head turns away.

**Guide section:** [symptom shutdown tolerate touch](#freeze-and-tolerate-under-handling)

##### Strategic avoidance of a person

Quietly leaves the room or hides when a specific person approaches — pre-empting unwanted handling after touch saturation.

**Linked patterns:** Fear reactive, Hyper-vigilant

**Confusable drivers:** Owner dynamics, Trauma & security-first

**Distinguish from:** Not aloofness or independence — the avoidance is person-specific and follows a history of overridden boundaries. Bond erodes with the people avoided.

**Substitution:** Let the dog opt out; make that person a source of calm space and choice, not pursuit. Rebuild with earned, consent-led contact.

**Decoupling:** Do not chase, corner, or lure the dog out to be petted — that confirms the person cannot be escaped.

**Proactive guidance:** Reduce handling volume from the avoided person; three-second pause; reward voluntary approach only.

**Guide section:** [symptom strategic avoidance](#strategic-avoidance-of-a-person)

##### Frantic greeting arousal

Helicopter tail, jumping, spinning at arrivals — matches handler energy often.

**Linked patterns:** Frenetic arousal, Anxious attachment

**Confusable drivers:** Owner dynamics, Entitlement & hardship, Age & development

**Distinguish from:** Fix owner matching arousal first. Adolescent testing vs entitled adult — age and hardship calibration.

**Substitution:** Neutral home return — wait for four on floor before engagement.

**Decoupling:** Do not praise the moment of highest arousal — see correction-praise trap.

**Proactive guidance:** Front door and home return protocol; collar snatch if jumping persists after calm handler.

**Guide section:** [symptom helicopter greeting](#frantic-greeting-arousal)

##### Repeated nudging or mouthing for contact

Nose bumps, mouthing hands — demand or anxious contact-seeking.

**Linked patterns:** Frenetic arousal, Anxious attachment

**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Age & development

**Distinguish from:** Puppy exploration fades with structure. Adult persistent mouthing — standard slipped or insecurity loop.

**Substitution:** Hold or toy in mouth for retrievers; Chin for calm contact script.

**Decoupling:** Withhold engagement during nudge — reward nominated behaviour only.

**Proactive guidance:** Guide Chin before the mouth finds skin.

**Guide section:** [symptom nudge mouth bump](#repeated-nudging-or-mouthing-for-contact)

#### Directed at: Environment

##### Obsessive surface or object licking

Fixated licking of floors, furniture, or objects — often scent or fixation, not attachment.

**Linked patterns:** Fixation loop, Frustration reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Breed expression

**Distinguish from:** Scenthound nose-led investigation is breed expression until it becomes a locked loop the dog cannot break. Attachment licking targets handler skin, not the floor.

**Substitution:** Scent puzzle, scatter feed, or structured nose work for hounds. Alternate visual job for fixation-prone herding types.

**Decoupling:** Remove access to the rehearsed surface during rehab; offer the substitute outlet before the environment triggers the loop.

**Proactive guidance:** Disengagement cue before fixation locks — see distraction processing. Butt push or leash accountability if entitlement rehearsal.

**Guide section:** [symptom compulsive lick environment](#obsessive-surface-or-object-licking)

##### Guarding a safe space or person

Stiffens or growls when approached on a crate, bed, or lap — defending the last boundary after feeling touch-vulnerable everywhere else.

**Linked patterns:** Fear reactive, Territorial vigilance

**Confusable drivers:** Entitlement & hardship, Trauma & security-first

**Distinguish from:** Insecurity-driven safe-space guarding (soft, defensive, follows touch saturation) differs from entitled resource claiming (stiff, forward, privileged history). Read the history and body.

**Substitution:** Restore whole-house consent so the dog does not need one anchor. Teach off/place with earned access; never reach into the safe space to force contact.

**Decoupling:** Do not punish the growl — it is the warning you want kept. Do not corner the dog on its bed or lap.

**Proactive guidance:** Approach low and side-on; invite off the space rather than reaching in; reduce the touch pressure that drove the anchoring.

**Guide section:** [symptom guard safe space](#guarding-a-safe-space-or-person-1)

##### Pacing boundaries

Repeated patrol of fence line or room perimeter — vigilance or frustration.

**Linked patterns:** Hyper-vigilant, Territorial vigilance, Frustration reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Breed expression

**Distinguish from:** Guard breed patrol is context — locked pacing without settle needs job and structure.

**Substitution:** Assigned place or job; drain tank with legitimate work before denial.

**Decoupling:** Block rehearsable patrol routes during rehab if needed; reward settle at place.

**Proactive guidance:** Nominate place before arousal builds at the boundary.

**Guide section:** [symptom pacing perimeter](#pacing-boundaries)

##### Locked stare at trigger

Sustained stare before lunge — fixation precursor.

**Linked patterns:** Fixation loop, Barrier frustration, Fear reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Breed expression

**Distinguish from:** Brief look with loose body is distraction processing — not fixation.

**Substitution:** Disengagement before lock; alternate job by instinct — fetch or scent.

**Decoupling:** Increase distance before trigger stacks; do not reward stare with forward movement.

**Proactive guidance:** Butt push or leash jerk inside one-second window when body stiffens.

**Guide section:** [symptom stare lock trigger](#locked-stare-at-trigger)

##### Leash or fence lunge

Explosive lunge when access blocked — barrier frustration primary.

**Linked patterns:** Barrier frustration, Fixation loop, Fear reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Skill gap — never taught, Entitlement & hardship

**Distinguish from:** Fear reactive needs distance; frustration entitlement needs leash accountability — hardship component.

**Substitution:** Distance for fear; leash accountability and collar choice for frustration — not treat-only.

**Decoupling:** Do not rehearse lunging at the same fence line daily without structure.

**Proactive guidance:** Leash handling, butt push, meetings on leash until social maturity.

**Guide section:** [symptom barrier lunge](#leash-or-fence-lunge)

##### Destruction when outlet denied

Chewing, digging, shredding when bored or blocked — frustration reactive.

**Linked patterns:** Frustration reactive, Separation stress

**Confusable drivers:** Age & development, Skill gap — never taught

**Distinguish from:** Puppy teething vs adult outburst when denied walk or attention.

**Substitution:** Legitimate job before denial — walk, scent, dig box for terriers.

**Decoupling:** Nothing for free — access earned after calm.

**Proactive guidance:** Drain tank first; then deny without surprise.

**Guide section:** [symptom destructive outburst](#destruction-when-outlet-denied)

##### Compulsive digging

Digging beyond breed outlet — frustration or terrier drive without structure.

**Linked patterns:** Frustration reactive, Fixation loop

**Confusable drivers:** Breed expression

**Distinguish from:** Terrier dig is breed — assign dig box; compulsive garden destruction needs structure.

**Substitution:** Designated dig pit or hunt box; structured search games.

**Decoupling:** Block rehearsable garden patches; redirect to assigned zone before denial.

**Proactive guidance:** Nominate dig zone; reward use of assigned outlet.

**Guide section:** [symptom digging compulsive](#compulsive-digging)

#### Directed at: General

##### Lip licking under stress

Single or brief lip licks — displacement signal, not necessarily a compulsive loop.

**Linked patterns:** Handler-sensitive, Fear reactive

**Confusable drivers:** Age & development, Neuro stress loop

**Distinguish from:** One flick after a correction is read context — not the same as repetitive handler licking that worsens under No/Stop.

**Substitution:** Lower handler energy; create space; small win before re-asking.

**Decoupling:** Do not scold the lip lick — it is information. Change what happens next.

**Proactive guidance:** Three-second pause; read what happened in the second before.

**Guide section:** [symptom lip lick displacement](#lip-licking-under-stress)

##### Distress vocalising when left alone

Whining, howling, barking when handler departs — separation stress, not velcro in room.

**Linked patterns:** Separation stress

**Confusable drivers:** Owner dynamics, Skill gap — never taught

**Distinguish from:** Velcro when handler present is anxious\_attachment — different pattern row. Camera or live monitor: true distress shows pacing, panting, drooling, or chewing at exits; demand vocalisation often whines, pauses to listen, whines again, then settles when it fails.

**Substitution:** Calm departure ritual; earned independence; safe den — not flooding.

**Decoupling:** Do not return and soothe mid-panic — teaches panic gets reunion. Re-enter only on settled quiet; a live feed helps time that second.

**Proactive guidance:** Short departures with wins; start with brief silence required before return, then build duration; optional camera to confirm demand vs true anxiety.

**Guide section:** [symptom vocal demand alone](#distress-vocalising-when-left-alone)

## Appendix C: Problem Finder

Every situation and problem the [Problem Finder](#chapter-21-the-problem-finder) covers, with the guidance for each level of impact and the guide sections to read.

### Impact levels

- **1**: Minor annoyance
- **2**: Noticeable but manageable
- **3**: Affecting daily life
- **4**: Stressful or embarrassing in public
- **5**: Safety concern or hard to live with

### Situations

#### On walks or out in public

Lead pulling, recall, reactivity, or embarrassment when you are out and about.

**Problems covered:** Pulling on the lead, Won't come when called, Lunging or reactive on walks, Issues with other dogs

#### At home

Barking, doors, visitors, separation, yard boundaries, impulse, or touch and handling indoors.

**Problems covered:** Barking or vocal behaviour, Door and visitor behaviour, Distress when left alone, Keeping them in the yard, Stealing food or rushing doors, Repetitive licking, chewing, or self-soothing, Touch sensitivity or handling avoidance

#### Around people or other dogs

Jumping on guests, anxiety, touch sensitivity, repetitive soothing, or trouble with other dogs in social situations.

**Problems covered:** Jumping up on people, Anxious or fearful, Touch sensitivity or handling avoidance, Issues with other dogs, Lunging or reactive on walks, Repetitive licking, chewing, or self-soothing

#### New dog or general basics

Puppy foundations, adolescent testing, or general manners and obedience.

**Problems covered:** Puppy or adolescent basics, General obedience and manners, Won't come when called

### Problems

#### Pulling on the lead

A dog that drags you down the street is usually telling you they do not yet see you as the one setting pace and direction. With the right collar, leash mechanics, and clear accountability, walks become calm and predictable — often faster than people expect.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Even a light pull is worth fixing early — it is easier before it becomes a habit.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** You are not alone; most owners start here, and structure fixes it quickly.
- **Affecting daily life:** When every walk feels like a battle, targeted leash work restores enjoyment for both of you.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Public embarrassment on walks is common — and very workable with consistent standards.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Strong pullers can be a safety risk; firm leash accountability and collar choice matter here.

**Guide sections:** [Leash accountability](#guide-training--leash), [Collar selection](#guide-training--collar-selection), [Leash handling](#biomechanical-handling)

#### Won't come when called

Recall is not a trick — it is trust that you will follow through when it matters. Building a reliable come-when-called starts with clear expectations, the right reward timing, and proofing in real-world situations.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** A patchy recall is normal; tightening structure now prevents bigger problems later.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Inconsistent recall usually means the dog has learned coming back is optional.
- **Affecting daily life:** When you cannot trust them off-lead, access and freedom stay limited — that can change.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Being the person shouting in the park is frustrating; clear standards fix the pattern.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Bolting or ignoring recall near roads is a serious safety issue — prioritise this with Warwick.

**Guide sections:** [Real-world expectations](#guide-leadership--expectations), [Go-get recall method](#the-go-get-method-for-recall-training), [Road safety](#road-safety-the-absolute-boundary-rural-nz)

#### Lunging or reactive on walks

Reactivity on lead often looks like aggression but is frequently frustration, fixation, or unclear boundaries. Interrupting the pattern, resetting body language, and teaching calm accountability on the leash are the foundation.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Early lunging or staring is worth addressing before it escalates.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Reactive moments on walks are common — structure reduces the frequency quickly.
- **Affecting daily life:** When walks are avoided because of reactions, targeted work restores confidence.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Public incidents are embarrassing and stressful; you are not failing — the dog needs clearer leadership.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Serious reactivity near triggers needs structured intervention; do not wait this out alone.

**Guide sections:** [Fixation and reactivity interruption](#guide-training--butt-push), [Leash accountability](#guide-training--leash), [Dog meetings on leash](#leash-on-for-dog-meetings--until-social-maturity)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Barrier frustration, Fixation loop

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Leash or fence lunge, Locked stare at trigger

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Entitlement & hardship, Breed expression, Trauma & security-first

#### Barking or vocal behaviour

Excessive barking is usually the dog practising a job you did not assign — alerting, demanding attention, or rehearsing arousal. Clear interruption, earned quiet, and consistent standards reduce vocal habits without suppressing normal communication.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Occasional barking is normal; persistent patterns are what we shape.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Frequent yapping at home or on walks responds well to structured interruption.
- **Affecting daily life:** When barking disrupts daily life or neighbours, it is time for a clear plan.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Public barking or embarrassment in shared spaces is workable with consistent correction.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Non-stop or aggressive vocalising needs firm structure — Warwick can calibrate the approach.

**Guide sections:** [Barking and fixation interruption](#guide-training--butt-push), [Verbal correction](#guide-training--verbal-correction), [Earned access and calm standards](#guide-training--access)

#### Jumping up on people

Jumping is a greeting habit the dog has been allowed to rehearse. Teaching a calm default at thresholds and greetings — with clear correction and follow-through — replaces excitement with manners visitors will notice.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Puppy jumping is common; fixing it early saves years of repetition.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Jumping on family is annoying but very fixable with consistent standards.
- **Affecting daily life:** When guests cannot visit comfortably, greeting structure becomes a priority.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Embarrassing jumps on strangers in public respond quickly to collar and accountability work.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Large or forceful jumpers can knock people over — address this with clear physical boundaries.

**Guide sections:** [Jumping and collar snatch](#guide-training--collar-snatch), [Front door protocol](#guide-leadership--front-door), [Earned access](#guide-training--access)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Frenetic arousal

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Frantic greeting arousal, Repeated nudging or mouthing for contact

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Owner dynamics, Entitlement & hardship, Age & development

#### Anxious or fearful

Fear and anxiety are not fixed traits — they are responses that change with calm leadership, predictable structure, and calibrated correction. Understanding whether you are seeing true trauma or rehearsed worry helps set the right pace.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Mild nervousness often improves as the dog learns you are a steady leader.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Noticeable fear on walks or at home benefits from structure before it becomes entrenched.
- **Affecting daily life:** When anxiety limits where you can go or what you can do, targeted rehabituation helps.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** A dog that embarrasses or worries you in public still needs advocacy, not pity — clarity helps.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Severe fear, shutdown, or panic needs careful calibration; Warwick will match intensity to the dog.

**Guide sections:** [Reading stress signals](#symptom-glossary), [Trauma vs everyday fear](#trauma-signals), [Driver calibration](#behavior-driver-calibration), [Rehabilitation patterns](#guide-understanding--rehabilitation-patterns), [Calm handler mindset](#guide-leadership--owner-mindset)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Handler-sensitive, Fear reactive, Hyper-vigilant

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Whale eye when handler looms, Lip licking under stress, Submissive urination on greeting, Freeze-and-tolerate under handling, Strategic avoidance of a person

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Trauma & security-first, Owner dynamics, Skill gap — never taught

#### Distress when left alone

Separation distress often reflects unclear pack structure and rehearsed panic. Building independence through earned access, calm departures, and consistent expectations reduces clingy or destructive alone-time behaviour.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Mild whining when you leave can be shaped before it becomes a full pattern.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Regular distress signals mean the dog has not learned alone-time is normal yet.
- **Affecting daily life:** When you cannot leave the house comfortably, separation structure is the focus.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Destructive or noisy alone behaviour affects neighbours and your peace of mind — it is fixable.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Severe panic, self-harm, or escape attempts need structured intervention soon.

**Guide sections:** [Earned access and independence](#guide-training--access), [Reducing dependency](#self-regulation-around-other-dogs), [Daily structure](#guide-daily-life--daily)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Separation stress

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Distress vocalising when left alone, Destruction when outlet denied

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Skill gap — never taught, Owner dynamics

#### Door and visitor behaviour

Chaos at the door — barking, rushing, jumping on guests — is one of the most common owner frustrations. Threshold work, front-door protocol, and clear accountability turn arrivals into calm, predictable events.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Excitement at the door is normal; teaching a calm default early pays off.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Regular door chaos is a training gap, not a personality flaw.
- **Affecting daily life:** When you dread visitors arriving, front-door structure should be top priority.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Embarrassing greetings make social life harder — guests will notice the change quickly.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Dogs that bolt through doors or mob guests create safety risks — firm thresholds matter.

**Guide sections:** [Front door protocol](#guide-leadership--front-door), [Earned access](#guide-training--access), [Jumping and greetings](#guide-training--collar-snatch)

#### Stealing food or rushing doors

Impulse problems — counter-surfing, bolting through doors, snatching — mean the dog has learned boundaries are negotiable. Clear interruption, nothing-for-free standards, and follow-through rebuild self-control.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Occasional snatching is a habit worth interrupting early.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Regular food stealing or door dashing responds to consistent impulse work.
- **Affecting daily life:** When impulse behaviour disrupts meals or daily routines, structure becomes essential.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Public snatching or door bolting is embarrassing and preventable with clear standards.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Dangerous dashing near roads or aggressive resource guarding needs immediate attention.

**Guide sections:** [Earned access and impulse](#guide-training--access), [Foundation pillars](#four-pillars-of-success), [Road and threshold safety](#road-safety-the-absolute-boundary-rural-nz)

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Destruction when outlet denied

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Entitlement & hardship, Skill gap — never taught

#### Keeping them in the yard

Staying on your property is a combination of recall, respect for boundaries, and earned freedom — not just fencing. Building reliable containment behaviour means the dog understands where their world ends and yours begins.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Occasional boundary testing is normal; clear standards prevent it becoming a habit.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** A dog that wanders the property line needs clearer access rules and recall proofing.
- **Affecting daily life:** When you cannot trust them in the yard, freedom and peace of mind are limited.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Chasing passers-by or escaping in front of neighbours is stressful — and very workable.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Dogs that bolt from the property create serious safety risks — prioritise boundary and recall work.

**Guide sections:** [Earned access and boundaries](#guide-training--access), [Real-world proofing](#guide-leadership--expectations), [Recall foundations](#the-go-get-method-for-recall-training)

#### Puppy or adolescent basics

Young dogs need establishment before adult standards — toilet training, daily rhythm, hunger-driven behavioral design, and check-in conditioning. Structure the environment so the right choice is easy before problems become entrenched habits.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Early weeks are the easiest time to set standards that last a lifetime.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Adolescent testing is normal; consistent structure gets you through it cleanly.
- **Affecting daily life:** When puppy chaos is overwhelming daily life, a focused foundation plan helps.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** An out-of-control adolescent in public is common — and responds fast to clear leadership.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Biting, bolting, or dangerous puppy behaviour needs firm calibration from the start.

**Guide sections:** [8-week separation](#the-8-week-separation-adjustment), [Rewards and hunger setup](#guide-training--rewards), [Age × temperament](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks)

#### Issues with other dogs

Dog-to-dog problems range from over-excitement to genuine reactivity. Reading social signals, managing meetings on and off leash, and teaching disengagement give your dog a calmer social world.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Rough play or over-greeting is common — early structure prevents escalation.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Regular friction with other dogs benefits from clearer social rules.
- **Affecting daily life:** When you avoid other dogs entirely, reactivity work can reopen that world.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Public incidents with other dogs are stressful; you need a plan, not avoidance.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Fights or serious aggression toward dogs need structured intervention — do not manage this alone.

**Guide sections:** [Dog meetings](#when-dogs-meet-play-correction-and-real-conflict), [Meetings on leash](#leash-on-for-dog-meetings--until-social-maturity), [Reactivity interruption](#guide-training--butt-push)

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Social dominance (dog-dog), Age & development

#### General obedience and manners

Sit, wait, heel, attention on the handler — these are not tricks but the language of daily life. When basics are inconsistent, everything else is harder. Clear structure and follow-through make manners reliable.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Patchy obedience is a great place to start — small wins compound quickly.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Inconsistent commands usually mean the dog has learned cues are optional.
- **Affecting daily life:** When daily life feels chaotic because basics are missing, foundations are the priority.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** A dog that ignores you in public reflects a training gap, not a lost cause.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Dangerous disobedience near roads or in high-stakes moments needs urgent structure.

**Guide sections:** [Foundation pillars](#four-pillars-of-success), [Say it once](#1-say-it-once--hear-it-then-enforce-it), [Daily structure](#guide-daily-life--daily)

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Skill gap — never taught

#### Repetitive licking, chewing, or self-soothing

Compulsive licking of handler or self, paw chewing, and similar repetitive soothing — often insecurity endorphin release, not defiance. Route through driver calibration, then the symptom index for handler vs self variants.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** Occasional licking is normal; persistent loops worth addressing with substitution, not repeated Stop.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Handler-licking and self-licking need different decoupling rules — identify the target first.
- **Affecting daily life:** When soothing behaviours disrupt daily contact or sleep, substitution playbook applies after driver check.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** Embarrassing or constant licking in public — workable once drivers and pattern are identified.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Self-lick with bald patches or hot spots — vet rule-out before behavioural plan alone.

**Guide sections:** [Driver calibration](#behavior-driver-calibration), [Symptom expression index](#symptom-expression-index), [Worked example: handler licking](#worked-example-compulsive-handler-licking-golden-retriever), [Rehabilitation patterns](#guide-understanding--rehabilitation-patterns)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Anxious attachment, Handler-sensitive, Frustration reactive

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Compulsive licking of handler, Compulsive self-licking, Persistent paw chewing, Obsessive surface or object licking

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Entitlement & hardship, Breed expression, Owner dynamics, Trauma & security-first

#### Touch sensitivity or handling avoidance

A dog that tolerates rather than enjoys petting, ducks the reaching hand, or slips away from certain people is often touch-saturated — over-handled to the point that contact became a demand. Left unread, a please-driven dog shuts down and stops signalling. Consent-led handling and reduced touch volume rebuild a genuine bond.

**By impact:**

- **Minor annoyance:** A dog that sometimes moves away from petting is telling you something — reading it early prevents avoidance becoming a habit.
- **Noticeable but manageable:** Regular ducking, leaving, or tolerating without enjoyment responds well to the consent test and reduced handling.
- **Affecting daily life:** When a dog actively avoids family members or hides, touch saturation and shutdown are worth addressing before the bond erodes.
- **Stressful or embarrassing in public:** A dog that freezes and endures handling looks calm but is often flooded — this is workable once everyone respects consent.
- **Safety concern or hard to live with:** Stiffening, growling, or snapping when approached or handled is a safety signal — do not punish it; prioritise this with Warwick.

**Guide sections:** [The three-second pause](#the-three-second-pause), [Touch saturation & consent test](#touch-saturation-and-the-consent-test), [Learned helplessness](#learned-helplessness-the-shutdown-dog), [Symptom expression index](#symptom-expression-index)

**Stress-looping patterns to consider:** Handler-sensitive, Fear reactive

**Symptom expressions to consider:** Freeze-and-tolerate under handling, Strategic avoidance of a person, Guarding a safe space or person

**Behaviour drivers to consider:** Owner dynamics, Trauma & security-first, Breed expression

## Appendix D: Breed Compendium

The breed reference used by the tools in [Part IV](#part-iv-tools-and-resources): 183 breeds and named crosses grouped into nine temperament types. Scores describe breed tendencies, never an individual dog.

### Temperament types

#### Clingy & people-focused

Bonds intensely and is highly responsive to affection — but sensitive to harsh rejection or corrections delivered with frustration. Calm, matter-of-fact energy; rebuild quickly after a reset. Please-driven dogs tolerate over-handling rather than signalling, so watch for touch saturation and shutdown.

**Personality and drive:** Bonds intensely to people and reads handler emotion closely. Sensitive to harsh rejection, cold withdrawal, or corrections delivered with frustration — the delivery matters as much as the rule. Rebuild warmth quickly after a reset; structure without affection can read as abandonment.

**Working style and energy:** People-pleasing engine — cooperative, engagement-oriented, often highly food- or affection-motivated. May ignore treats when social connection or access to you is the real currency. Responds best to calm approval for calm behaviour, not excited praise during reactions.

**Physical build:** Medium athletic companion build — level topline, moderate angulation; retriever, spaniel, or stocky bull-companion silhouettes with short to medium coat.

**Sensitivities:** People-focused types often amplify stress when handler mood is inconsistent — cold withdrawal, excitement-matching, or indulgence without structure. Please-driven dogs tolerate over-handling rather than signalling, so watch for touch saturation and shutdown.

**Breeds of this type:** Staffordshire Bull Terrier (Staffy), American Staffordshire Terrier, Pit Bull type, American Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever, Flat-Coated Retriever, Chesapeake Bay Retriever, Curly-Coated Retriever, Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, Boxer, Vizsla, Wirehaired Vizsla, Weimaraner, Cocker Spaniel, Springer Spaniel, Brittany Spaniel, Clumber Spaniel, Field Spaniel, Pointer (English / GSP), German Wirehaired Pointer, Irish Setter, Gordon Setter, English Setter, Hungarian Pointer, Portuguese Water Dog, Lagotto Romagnolo, Dalmatian, Poodle (Standard), Miniature Poodle, Toy Poodle, Labradoodle / Groodle, Cavoodle / Spoodle, Cockapoo, Schnoodle, Bernedoodle, Retrodoodle / Sheepadoodle, Bulldog (British), Bull Terrier, Hungarian Pumi

#### Sighthound & chase type

Calm, even lazy at rest — then an explosive chase trigger when movement flashes. Independent and soft-tempered: harsh corrections shut them down, and no correction outruns the chase once it has launched. Manage the trigger window.

**Personality and drive:** Soft-tempered and independent — not stubborn, but not biddable by nagging. Calm, even lazy at rest; shuts down under harsh or repeated correction. Once the chase launches, no correction outruns it — manage the trigger window, not the aftermath.

**Working style and energy:** Visual/chase engine — explosive when movement flashes, low interest in repetition drills. Wants brief bursts of speed, then rest. Manage environment and line-of-sight; do not expect sustained heel focus beside triggers.

**Physical build:** Lean sighthound silhouette — narrow head, deep chest, extreme tuck-up, long fine-boned legs; coat short and smooth to long and silky by breed.

**Sensitivities:** Soft-tempered and chase-driven — movement flashes and harsh correction delivery are common trigger paths; manage triggers before the chase launches.

**Breeds of this type:** Greyhound, Whippet, Italian Greyhound, Saluki, Borzoi, Afghan Hound, Irish Wolfhound, Scottish Deerhound, Lurcher, Staghound (NZ hunting type), Pharaoh Hound, Ibizan Hound, Azawakh, Sloughi

#### Spitz & sled type

Independent, endurance-driven, and famously vocal. Weak default recall, strong escape instincts — fences and thresholds matter. Earned access and structured outlets beat repetition drills.

**Personality and drive:** Independent and not biddable by default — does not respond to repetition nagging or moral scolding. Vocal when frustrated or under-stimulated. Respects calm structure and earned access, not endless drilling.

**Working style and energy:** Endurance engine — wants distance, exploration, and job-like outlets. Weak default recall; strong roam and escape drive. Thresholds, fences, and structured access beat obedience repetition for its own sake.

**Physical build:** Spitz silhouette — prick ears, fox-like head, dense double coat, and compact to medium proportions; tail curled or plumed over the back.

**Sensitivities:** Independent and vocal — frustration from denied outlets and threshold breaches often precede stress loops.

**Breeds of this type:** Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute, Samoyed, Shiba Inu, Basenji, Keeshond, Norwegian Elkhound, Finnish Lapphund, Finnish Spitz, German Spitz, Japanese Spitz, Eurasier, Pomsky, Alaskan Klee Kai

#### Visual & herding type

Wired to track motion and prone to eye-lock fixation. Watch the stare before the lunge, favour access and environmental rewards, and avoid prolonged face-to-face gazing rituals.

**Personality and drive:** Alert and motion-sensitive — prone to eye-lock fixation and, in some lines, attachment distortion with prolonged face-to-face gazing. Needs calm leadership, not excitement-matching. Correct early; do not wait for the lunge.

**Working style and energy:** Motion-tracking engine — intercepts movement (feet, bikes, stock, children). Act at the stare before the body moves. Access and environmental rewards often land better than treat-chasing for dogs already wired to track.

**Physical build:** Agile herding build — quick direction changes, moderate bone, weather-resistant coat; from compact collie types to large deep-chested NZ workers.

**Sensitivities:** Motion-sensitive — visual fixation and handler energy matching are primary trigger paths before reactivity surfaces.

**Breeds of this type:** Border Collie, NZ Heading Dog, NZ Huntaway, Rough / Smooth Collie, Bearded Collie, Australian Shepherd, Mini Australian Shepherd, Australian Cattle Dog (Blue Heeler), Kelpie, Koolie, Shetland Sheepdog (Sheltie), Old English Sheepdog, Welsh Corgi (Pembroke / Cardigan), Swedish Vallhund, Belgian Shepherd (Groenendael / Tervuren), Briard, Bouvier des Flandres, Puli, Polish Lowland Sheepdog, Border Collie x Huntaway, White Swiss Shepherd

#### Terrier & high-drive working type

Needs sniff, run, and problem-solving outlets. Denied those, frustration surfaces as fixation, reactivity, or destruction. Access training is often the right currency.

**Personality and drive:** Frustration-prone when under-stimulated — fixation and reactivity surface as "naughty" behaviour, not bad character. Tenacious and bold; needs clarity and earned access, not indulgence or excuse-making.

**Working style and energy:** High-drive engine — requires sniff, run, and problem-solving outlets daily. Access training is often the right currency; denied outlets become destruction, digging, or leash fixation. Brief, intense work sessions beat long dull drills.

**Physical build:** Compact muscular terrier frame — short back, strong jaw, and wiry or harsh coat; Jack Russell to Airedale spans small to large within the same dense build.

**Sensitivities:** High-drive — denied sniff, dig, or problem-solving outlets commonly trigger fixation and frustration patterns.

**Breeds of this type:** Jack Russell Terrier, Parson Russell Terrier, Fox Terrier, Border Terrier, Cairn Terrier, West Highland White Terrier (Westie), Scottish Terrier, Airedale Terrier, Patterdale Terrier, Lakeland Terrier, Bedlington Terrier, Manchester Terrier, Norfolk / Norwich Terrier, Rat Terrier, Welsh Terrier, Irish Terrier, Kerry Blue Terrier, Soft-Coated Wheaten Terrier, Standard Schnauzer, Miniature Schnauzer, Pig Dog (NZ hunting cross), Bull Arab, Catahoula Leopard Dog, Spaniel-cross working dog

#### Scenthound & nose-led type

When the nose engages, the ears switch off — recall fails on scent, not defiance. Usually strongly food-motivated; reserve a high-value treat and train recall before the nose locks on. Vocal baying is communication, not naughtiness.

**Personality and drive:** Not defiant when the nose engages — ears switch off and the world narrows to scent. Baying and vocalising are communication, not spite. Patient handler energy; do not moralise what is drive, not attitude.

**Working style and energy:** Scent-first engine — recall fails on trail, not disobedience. Train recall before the nose locks; earned sniff breaks are powerful currency. Food-motivated when the nose is free — use that, do not fight the nose all walk.

**Physical build:** Scenthound silhouette — long muzzle, long pendulous ears, and stamina-built body; from compact beagle to massive bloodhound proportions.

**Sensitivities:** Nose-led — recall and engagement failures on scent are drive, not attitude; separation less often the primary trigger than frustration.

**Breeds of this type:** Beagle, Harrier Hound, Dachshund, Miniature Dachshund, Basset Hound, Bloodhound, Foxhound (English / American), Coonhound, Otterhound, Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen, Hamiltonstövare, Beagle-cross

#### Guardian & protection type

Prone to vigilance. Rewarding every wary glance with reassurance entrenches anxiety — calm leadership and earned access matter more than comfort-talk.

**Personality and drive:** Vigilant and territory-aware — reads threat in neutral stimuli. Rewarding every wary glance with reassurance entrenches anxiety. Calm leadership and consistent structure matter more than comfort-talk or excitement about "protectiveness".

**Working style and energy:** Patrol-and-assess engine — alert barking is job behaviour, not random noise. Needs structured exposure to triggers, not isolation. Earned access and calm handler neutrality reduce vigilance over time.

**Physical build:** Powerful guardian silhouette — broad skull, deep chest, strong neck, and imposing shoulder line; short to medium dense coat.

**Sensitivities:** Vigilant — novel stimuli, strangers, and territory cues commonly trigger patrol and alert patterns.

**Breeds of this type:** German Shepherd, Belgian Malinois, Rottweiler, Doberman, Mastiff (English / Bull / Neapolitan), Bullmastiff, Cane Corso, Boerboel, Dogue de Bordeaux, Presa Canario, Rhodesian Ridgeback, Akita, Shar Pei, Chow Chow, Tibetan Mastiff, Dogo Argentino, Beauceron, Giant Schnauzer, Black Russian Terrier

#### Giant & livestock guardian

Independent decision-makers bred to work without instruction, and slow to mature. Their size makes leash manners, thresholds, and calm greetings non-negotiable from day one — habits cute in a puppy are dangerous at sixty kilograms.

**Personality and drive:** Independent decision-makers — slow to mature, not defiant but unconvinced. Bred to work without instruction; structure must make compliance worthwhile. Do not confuse independence with dominance requiring confrontation.

**Working style and energy:** Work-alone engine — patrols boundaries, assesses without asking permission. Low biddability for pointless repetition; earned access and consistent structure carry more weight than drill sergeant energy.

**Physical build:** Giant livestock or draft silhouette — heavy bone, broad chest, thick coat common; among the largest height and weight in domestic dogs.

**Sensitivities:** Slow to mature — early indulgence and weak thresholds become dangerous at full size; novelty and stranger exposure need structure.

**Breeds of this type:** Great Dane, Anatolian Shepherd / Maremma, Great Pyrenees (Pyrenean Mountain Dog), Komondor, Kuvasz, Bernese Mountain Dog, Greater Swiss Mountain Dog, Newfoundland, St Bernard, Leonberger, Pyrenean Mastiff, Caucasian Shepherd, Central Asian Shepherd, Estrela Mountain Dog

#### Small breed

Carrying, hand-feeding, and excusing pushy behaviour because it is "cute" often produces a dog that cannot tolerate boundaries from anyone — including you. Easy to scoop up and over-handle, so touch saturation and learned-helplessness shutdown are common when boundaries go unread.

**Personality and drive:** Often excused as "cute" — carried, hand-fed, and allowed to push because of size. Same standard as big dogs; intolerance of boundaries from anyone, including you, is a common outcome of indulgence.

**Working style and energy:** Lower raw stamina but can be intensely persistent and demanding. Often over-handled — needs ground-level structure, not constant carrying. Treats and access still apply; do not substitute pity for training.

**Physical build:** Small companion silhouette — delicate fine bone, shorter muzzle common, and long or plush coat in many toy and lap types.

**Sensitivities:** Often over-handled — cute excuses for pushy behaviour amplify handler-mood and touch sensitivities. Boundaries get violated more because they are easy to pick up, so touch saturation and learned helplessness are real risks.

**Breeds of this type:** Chihuahua, Shih Tzu, Maltese, Pomeranian, Papillon, Bichon Frise, Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, King Charles Spaniel, Pug, French Bulldog, Boston Terrier, Yorkshire Terrier, Silky Terrier, Lhasa Apso, Pekingese, Havanese, Coton de Tulear, Miniature Pinscher, Brussels Griffon, Japanese Chin, Tibetan Spaniel, Chinese Crested, Affenpinscher, Maltese Shih Tzu cross, Chihuahua cross

### Score dimensions

| Dimension | Short label | What it measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overall IQ | IQ | Composite obedience/working intelligence — how quickly the breed typically learns commands and performs in structured training. Top-tier breeds are ranked from Stanley Coren's research. |
| Instinctive | Inst | Innate talent for the work the breed was developed for, scored for strength (1–10). Each breed profile also names the instinct type or blend (herding eye, chase, scent, guard, etc.). Not the same as protectiveness. |
| Adaptive | Adapt | Problem-solving and learning from experience without step-by-step instruction — figuring out puzzles, reading new situations, and generalising lessons on their own. |
| Working & obedience | Work | Responsiveness to handler direction during structured training — repetition learning, command reliability, and willingness to work cooperatively with a person. |
| Emotional intelligence | Emot | Social and emotional attunement to people — reading household mood, bonding intensity, and sensitivity to human emotion. Not the same as anxiety or neuroticism alone. |
| Spatial | Spat | Awareness of surroundings, distances, and object positions — navigation, visual memory, and spatial problem-solving in the environment. |
| Dominance | Dom | Tendency toward assertive or rank-seeking behaviour with people and other dogs — pushiness, guarding position, and challenging boundaries. The score shows strength; it is not a good/bad scale. |
| Protectiveness | Prot | Drive to guard household, territory, or family — alertness to strangers and vigilance. Distinct from guard instinct talent in the Inst column. |
| Potential neuroticism | Neur | Estimated baseline propensity for stress-looping. Each breed profile also lists the patterns that tend to express (separation, hyper-vigilance, handler-sensitivity, etc.). Handler-attuned breeds may present higher anxiety than the baseline when structure or warmth is inconsistent. Not a label for any individual dog. |
| Vocal / barking | Vocal | Typical vocal output — alert barking, baying, yapping, or habitual noise. The score shows how vocal the breed type tends to be; upbringing and structure strongly shape expression. |

### Instinct types

- **Herding eye:** Motion tracking, gather instinct, and eye-lock before movement (heeler nip — not protectiveness).
- **Chase:** Sighthound-style visual chase trigger and prey pursuit (lunge after movement flash).
- **Scent:** Nose-led tracking, trailing, and scent fixation (recall fails on scent, not defiance).
- **Guard:** Bred-for guarding, patrol, and territorial assessment talent (distinct from stress vigilance).
- **Retrieve:** Soft mouth, fetch, and people-oriented working partnership.
- **Hunt / dig:** Terrier-style earth work, vermin drive, and problem-solving hunt.
- **Sled / endurance:** Spitz-type endurance, independence, and long-range drive.
- **Companion:** People-focused companion drive rather than specialised field work.

**Epithet:** *The Velcro Heart*

**Trainer summary:** Bonds intensely and is highly responsive to affection — but sensitive to harsh rejection or corrections delivered with frustration. **Personality and drive:** Bonds intensely to people and reads handler emotion closely. **Epithet:** *The When the nose engages Spirit*

**Trainer summary:** When the nose engages, the ears switch off — recall fails on scent, not defiance. Usually strongly food-motivated; reserve a high-value treat and train recall before the nose locks on. Vocal baying is communication, not naughtiness.

**Personality and drive:** Not defiant when the nose engages — ears switch off and the world narrows to scent. Baying and vocalising are communication, not spite. Patient handler energy; do not moralise what is drive, not attitude.

**Working style and energy:** Scent-first engine — recall fails on trail, not disobedience. Train recall before the nose locks; earned sniff breaks are powerful currency. Food-motivated when the nose is free — use that, do not fight the nose all walk.

**Physical build and size:** ~29–34 kg. Large lean pack hound — short coat, long legs, and endurance-built frame.

- **Core Essence:** Not defiant when the nose engages — ears switch off and the world narrows to scent. Baying and vocalising are communication, not spite. Patient handler energy; do not moralise what is drive, not attitude.

#### Greyhound

*Sighthound & chase type · Large size · Estimated intelligence profile*

**Epithet:** *The Calm Spirit*

**Trainer summary:** Calm, even lazy at rest — then an explosive chase trigger when movement flashes. Independent and soft-tempered: harsh corrections shut them down, and no correction outruns the chase once it has launched. Manage the trigger window.

**Personality and drive:** Soft-tempered and independent — not stubborn, but not biddable by nagging. Calm, even lazy at rest; shuts down under harsh or repeated correction. Once the chase launches, no correction outruns it — manage the trigger window, not the aftermath.

**Working style and energy:** Visual/chase engine — explosive when movement flashes, low interest in repetition drills. Wants brief bursts of speed, then rest. Manage environment and line-of-sight; do not expect sustained heel focus beside triggers.

**Physical build and size:** ~27–32 kg. Large lean sighthound — deep chest, extreme tuck-up, long legs, and short smooth coat.

*Sighthound & chase type · Giant size · Estimated intelligence profile*

**Epithet:** *The Calm Spirit*

**Trainer summary:** Calm, even lazy at rest — then an explosive chase trigger when movement flashes. Independent and soft-tempered: harsh corrections shut them down, and no correction outruns the chase once it has launched. Manage the trigger window.

**Personality and drive:** Soft-tempered and independent — not stubborn, but not biddable by nagging. Calm, even lazy at rest; shuts down under harsh or repeated correction. Once the chase launches, no correction outruns it — manage the trigger window, not the aftermath.

**Working style and energy:** Visual/chase engine — explosive when movement flashes, low interest in repetition drills. Wants brief bursts of speed, then rest. Manage environment and line-of-sight; do not expect sustained heel focus beside triggers.

**Physical build and size:** ~35–50 kg. Giant rough sighthound — wiry coat, smaller head than Wolfhound, and tall deep-chested frame.

**Intelligence and temperament scores (1–10):**

| IQ | Inst | Adapt | Work | Emot | Spat | Dom | Prot | Neur | Vocal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | 9 | 5.2 | 4.6 | 6.8 | 5.8 | 3.5 | 3 | 5 | 3 |

**Instinct blend:** Chase 100%

**Stress-looping pattern blend:** Fear reactive 45%, Handler-sensitive 35%, Noise reactive 20%

**Stress-looping propensity (Moderate):** Some stress sensitivity is fairly common in this type.

**Sensitivities:** Soft-tempered and chase-driven — movement flashes and harsh correction delivery are common trigger paths; manage triggers before the chase launches.

| Sensitivity | Level | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Handler mood & tone | Elevated |  |
| Correction delivery | Elevated |  |
| Noise & sudden sound | Moderate |  |
| Movement & visual triggers | High |  |
| Separation & alone time | Moderate |  |
| Novelty & environment | Elevated |  |
| Touch & handling | Elevated |  |
| Strangers & greetings | Elevated |  |

**As a puppy:** Soft and easily startled — introduce novelty gradually; avoid harsh correction that shuts the dog down.

**As an adolescent:** Chase drive strengthens — line-of-sight management matters before off-lead access; one chase can rewrite the walk.

**Maturation:** Slow to mature — adult expectations may apply later than two years.

**Spirit reading:**

- **Core Essence:** Soft-tempered and independent — not stubborn, but not biddable by nagging.  Calm, even lazy at rest; shuts down under harsh or repeated correction.  Once the chase launches, no correction outruns it — manage the trigger window, not the aftermath.
- **In the Pack:** You are selective with your energy — affectionate on your terms, spectacular when something moves. You prefer calm company to chaos and dignity to drama.
- **Your Drive:** Visual/chase engine — explosive when movement flashes, low interest in repetition drills. Wants brief bursts of speed, then rest. Manage environment and line-of-sight; do not expect sustained heel focus beside triggers.
- **Body & Presence:** ~35–50 kg. Giant rough sighthound — wiry coat, smaller head than Wolfhound, and tall deep-chested frame.
- **Growth Edge:** Your shadow is the sudden launch — impulse can outrun politeness. Channel the chase into something worthy before the reflex takes the wheel. Some stress sensitivity is fairly common in this type.

*You were born to conserve, then astonish — rest is not laziness, it is strategy.*
