**Intelligence and temperament scores (1–10):**

| IQ | Inst | Adapt | Work | Emot | Spat | Dom | Prot | Neur | Vocal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.8 | 8 | 6.8 | 7 | 8.5 | 7 | 4.5 | 4.5 | 5 | 4 |

**Instinct blend:** Retrieve 100%

**Stress-looping pattern blend:** Separation stress 35%, Anxious attachment 35%, Handler-sensitive 30%

**Stress-looping propensity (Moderate):** Some stress sensitivity is fairly common in this type.

**Sensitivities:** People-focused types often amplify stress when handler mood is inconsistent — cold withdrawal, excitement-matching, or indulgence without structure. Please-driven dogs tolerate over-handling rather than signalling, so watch for touch saturation and shutdown.

| Sensitivity | Level | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Handler mood & tone | Elevated |  |
| Correction delivery | Moderate |  |
| Noise & sudden sound | Moderate |  |
| Movement & visual triggers | Moderate |  |
| Separation & alone time | Elevated |  |
| Novelty & environment | Moderate |  |
| Touch & handling | Moderate |  |
| Strangers & greetings | Moderate |  |

**As a puppy:** Bond forms fast — start structure early without cold withdrawal. Voluntary contact is fine; do not reward demanding paw or lean in training mode.

**As an adolescent:** Testing boundaries is common — hold the adult standard from seven months; excitement is not an excuse for pushy greetings or leash freelancing.

**Spirit reading:**

- **Core Essence:** Bonds intensely to people and reads handler emotion closely.  Sensitive to harsh rejection, cold withdrawal, or corrections delivered with frustration — the delivery matters as much as the rule.  Rebuild warmth quickly after a reset; structure without affection can read as abandonment.
- **In the Pack:** You read the room through the people in it — loyalty is your love language, and you would rather follow your person than explore alone. Warmth is your default; you just need boundaries that feel kind, not cold.
- **Your Drive:** People-pleasing engine — cooperative, engagement-oriented, often highly food- or affection-motivated. May ignore treats when social connection or access to you is the real currency. Responds best to calm approval for calm behaviour, not excited praise during reactions.
- **Body & Presence:** ~20–27 kg. Same scale as Vizsla — dense wiry golden coat, beard and eyebrows, and rugged athletic build.
- **Growth Edge:** Your chart warns against taking every mood personally — when someone needs space, it is not rejection. Practice resting your optimism without losing it. Some stress sensitivity is fairly common in this type.

*The universe assigned you a heart that stays — just remember you are whole even when the room is quiet.*

#### Yorkshire Terrier

*Small breed · Toy size · Coren intelligence rank 62*

**Epithet:** *The Pocket Executive*

**Trainer summary:** Carrying, hand-feeding, and excusing pushy behaviour because it is "cute" often produces a dog that cannot tolerate boundaries from anyone — including you. Easy to scoop up and over-handle, so touch saturation and learned-helplessness shutdown are common when boundaries go unread.

**Personality and drive:** Often excused as "cute" — carried, hand-fed, and allowed to push because of size. Same standard as big dogs; intolerance of boundaries from anyone, including you, is a common outcome of indulgence.

**Working style and energy:** Lower raw stamina but can be intensely persistent and demanding. Often over-handled — needs ground-level structure, not constant carrying. Treats and access still apply; do not substitute pity for training.

**Physical build and size:** ~2–3 kg. Toy terrier — long silky blue-and-tan coat, fine bone, and compact frame.

**Intelligence and temperament scores (1–10):**

| IQ | Inst | Adapt | Work | Emot | Spat | Dom | Prot | Neur | Vocal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.8 | 7.2 | 6.9 | 6.8 | 7.8 | 6.4 | 5.5 | 3.5 | 6.8 | 8.5 |

**Instinct blend:** Companion 100%

**Stress-looping pattern blend:** Anxious attachment 40%, Fear reactive 35%, Separation stress 25%

**Stress-looping propensity (Elevated):** Anxious or stress-looping tendencies are moderately common in this type — individual upbringing varies.

**Sensitivities:** Often over-handled — cute excuses for pushy behaviour amplify handler-mood and touch sensitivities. Boundaries get violated more because they are easy to pick up, so touch saturation and learned helplessness are real risks.

| Sensitivity | Level | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Handler mood & tone | Elevated |  |
| Correction delivery | Elevated |  |
| Noise & sudden sound | Moderate |  |
| Movement & visual triggers | Moderate |  |
| Separation & alone time | Elevated |  |
| Novelty & environment | Moderate |  |
| Touch & handling | Elevated |  |
| Strangers & greetings | Moderate |  |

**As a puppy:** Resist carrying, hand-feeding, and excusing pushy behaviour because of size — ground-level structure from the start.

**As an adolescent:** Demanding behaviours often peak if indulged early — same standard as a large dog from seven months onward.

**Spirit reading:**

- **Core Essence:** Often excused as "cute" — carried, hand-fed, and allowed to push because of size. Same standard as big dogs; intolerance of boundaries from anyone, including you, is a common outcome of indulgence. Anxious or stress-looping tendencies are moderately common in this type — individual upbringing varies.
- **In the Pack:** You have learned that charm opens doors — compact frame, full-size personality, and zero interest in being overlooked.
- **Your Drive:** Lower raw stamina but can be intensely persistent and demanding. Often over-handled — needs ground-level structure, not constant carrying. Treats and access still apply; do not substitute pity for training.
- **Body & Presence:** ~2–3 kg. Toy terrier — long silky blue-and-tan coat, fine bone, and compact frame.
- **Growth Edge:** Small does not mean fragile and cute does not mean without rules — boundaries keep your confidence healthy. worry-prone or stress-looping tendencies are moderately common in this type — individual upbringing varies.

*You were born to prove that presence is not measured in inches.*

### Instinct training leverage

#### Scent

**Scent-work is currency — not a heel competition.**

**Fixation:** Nose-led lock on dogs, posts, or trail — ears switch off; recall fails on scent, not defiance.

##### Scent chain: hand → hidden find

Scent your closed hand, let the dog investigate, then send to a hidden treat or toy. Reward the find — the nose job replaces staring at triggers.

**Use when:** Fixation on other dogs or environmental scent is building.

**Interrupts:** dog-dog fixation, barrier frustration, scent lock on walk

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [genetic leverage](#2-genetic-leverage-breed-blueprint), [access](#guide-training--access)

##### Proactive sniff release on walk

Grant a short, explicit sniff threshold before arousal peaks — at the start of the outing or after a trigger — then resume heel on your cue.

**Use when:** Nose-led types need decompression before cooperation returns.

**Interrupts:** pull toward scent, fixation loop on trail

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [sniff breaks](#heel-earns-the-sniff-break), [leash](#guide-training--leash)

##### Scatter search from daily ration

Spread part of the measured daily food in grass or a snuffle mat. Legitimate nose work drains the tank before you deny access.

**Use when:** Frustration when outlets are thin; substitute before denial.

**Interrupts:** frustration reactive, destructive outbursts when bored

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [rewards](#guide-training--rewards)

##### Assigned scent task as preferred reward

Use find-it, trailing, or container games as the payoff for calm check-ins or disengagement from triggers — not praise alone.

**Use when:** Social sessions where prey-drive fixation on other dogs is the failure point.

**Interrupts:** dog-dog fixation, fixation loop

**Life phases:** Adolescent, Adult

**Guide sections:** [genetic leverage](#2-genetic-leverage-breed-blueprint), [dog meetings](#when-dogs-meet-play-correction-and-real-conflict)

#### Hunt / dig

**Run, dig, and problem-solve — or frustration becomes fixation.**

**Fixation:** Denied sniff, dig, or chase outlets surface as yap, destruction, or locked stare — not bad character.

##### Backward running + floor proximity treats

Run backward down a hallway or open space; drop kibble at your feet when the dog orients. Movement pulls attention better than static lures on high-drive terriers.

**Use when:** Puppies and adolescents need owner orientation without face-to-face staring.

**Interrupts:** fixation on movement, poor check-in under arousal

**Life phases:** Puppy, Adolescent

**Guide sections:** [puppy behavior design](#behavioral-design-set-up-the-win), [puppy check in](#the-seven-second-check-in--puppy-establishment), [go get recall](#the-go-get-method-for-recall-training)

##### Assigned dig box / earthwork zone

Provide a legal dig pit or sand box before calling digging pathological. Drain the earth drive, then deny elsewhere without surprise.

**Use when:** Garden destruction or compulsive digging when outlets are denied.

**Interrupts:** frustration reactive, destructive outbursts

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [breed temperament](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application)

##### Puzzle scatter and problem-solving feed

Hide food in boxes, towels, or scatter lanes. Terriers need a job — boredom becomes yap and fixation quickly.

**Use when:** Under-stimulated days between structured walks.

**Interrupts:** frustration reactive, fixation loop

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [rewards](#guide-training--rewards)

##### Structured tug with wind-down

Short, rule-bound tug or chase games with a clear stop cue and post-play toilet or settle transition.

**Use when:** Prey-drive needs an outlet before calm proximity work.

**Interrupts:** frenetic arousal, barrier frustration

**Life phases:** Puppy, Adolescent, Adult

**Guide sections:** [puppy mouthing play](#mouthing-teething-and-appropriate-play), [access](#guide-training--access)

#### Chase

**Manage the trigger window — you cannot recall a launched chase.**

**Fixation:** Movement flash triggers explosive pursuit; once launched, correction is too late — pre-empt distance and arousal.

##### Trigger-window management

Increase distance before movement flashes; watch stiffening and stare-lock as precursors, not the lunge.

**Use when:** Sighthounds or chase-heavy mixes near runners, bikes, or fast dogs.

**Interrupts:** fixation loop, barrier frustration

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [dog ready stance](#reading-the-dogs-ready-stance), [leash](#guide-training--leash)

##### Low-arousal motion games with clear stop

Controlled chase games with start/stop cues in safe space — arousal on your terms, not ambient triggers.

**Use when:** Building engagement without letting ambient movement hijack the session.

**Interrupts:** frenetic arousal

**Life phases:** Puppy, Adolescent

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [training](#chapter-18-training--timing-leash-technique-and-corrections)

##### Pre-emptive distance before movement flash

Cross the street, arc wide, or pause until the trigger passes — do not test recall against a running target.

**Use when:** Recall fails on movement, not handler relationship.

**Interrupts:** dog-dog fixation, barrier frustration

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [leash](#guide-training--leash), [go get recall](#the-go-get-method-for-recall-training)

#### Herding eye

**Break eye-lock before the lunge — access beats stare-down.**

**Fixation:** Motion tracking and gather instinct — stiff stare at dogs, children, or wheels precedes nip or lunge.

##### Break visual lock at precursor

Interrupt stare-lock with spatial pressure or a reset word before movement commits — not prolonged face-to-face gazing.

**Use when:** Heeler-type fixation on motion or other dogs.

**Interrupts:** fixation loop, dog-dog fixation

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [dog ready stance](#reading-the-dogs-ready-stance), [breed temperament](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application)

##### Access and environmental reward

Earned continuation of walk, sniff, or play replaces praise cycles — environmental currency over handler drama.

**Use when:** Eye-lock breeds learn to negotiate for access if praise is over-delivered.

**Interrupts:** barrier frustration

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [rewards](#guide-training--rewards)

##### Nominate sit or place before movement

Proactive guidance: name the body position before the dog chooses to chase or gather — remove guesswork.

**Use when:** Structured exposures where motion triggers gather.

**Interrupts:** fixation loop

**Life phases:** Adolescent, Adult

**Guide sections:** [proactive guidance](#4-proactive-guidance-over-reactive-correction), [cue once](#1-say-it-once--hear-it-then-enforce-it)

#### Retrieve

**Mouth work and partnership — fetch as functional substitute.**

**Fixation:** Oral fixation and velcro bonding — carrying, mouthing, and handler focus seek a job for the mouth.

##### Mouth job (Hold soft toy)

Teach Hold with a soft toy as security blanket — neurological grounding through carry work, not suppression.

**Use when:** Anxious attachment, mouthing, or oral self-soothing loops.

**Interrupts:** anxious attachment, compulsive handler licking

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [genetic leverage](#2-genetic-leverage-breed-blueprint), [pattern playbook anxious attachment](#anxious-attachment-1)

##### Structured fetch with calm delivery

Fetch with clear start, delivery to hand, and settle — partnership outlet before denial.

**Use when:** High retrieve drive needs drain before calm threshold work.

**Interrupts:** frustration reactive, frenetic arousal

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [rewards](#guide-training--rewards)

##### Chin / Nose nomination

Proactive Chin or Nose touch for calm static contact — nominate the good before demand behaviours start.

**Use when:** Substituting for demand paw or mouthing at greetings.

**Interrupts:** anxious attachment, demand behaviours

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [proactive guidance](#4-proactive-guidance-over-reactive-correction), [context of contact](#the-context-of-contact-training-mode-vs-living-mode)

#### Guard

**Assigned patrol with earned access — not reassurance for every glance.**

**Fixation:** Vigilance at boundaries, strangers, and territory — patrol without structure becomes anxiety reinforcement.

##### Assigned patrol with start/stop

Structured perimeter check on cue — start and finish the job; calm leadership, not comfort-talk for every wary glance.

**Use when:** Guardian types patrol doors, fences, or windows obsessively.

**Interrupts:** territorial vigilance, hyper-vigilant scanning

**Life phases:** Adolescent, Adult

**Guide sections:** [front door](#guide-leadership--front-door), [pack guarding](#pack-guarding-the-bathroom-follow)

##### Earned access, not reassurance loops

Withhold engagement until calm coordination — do not reward every alert glance with soothing talk.

**Use when:** Vigilance breeds entrench anxiety when every scan gets reassurance.

**Interrupts:** territorial vigilance, handler-sensitive loops

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [breed temperament](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application), [love at the right time](#love-at-the-right-time), [trust not just love](#trust-not-just-love)

##### Threshold structure at doors and fence line

Place, wait, and release protocols at boundaries — patrol is on your schedule, not ambient triggers.

**Use when:** Barrier frustration at fence or door when access is blocked.

**Interrupts:** barrier frustration, territorial vigilance

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [front door](#guide-leadership--front-door), [access](#guide-training--access)

#### Sled / endurance

**Endurance first — then deny without surprise.**

**Fixation:** Pent-up distance drive and independence — weak default recall when under-exercised; escape and frustration spike.

##### Endurance outlet before denial

Long structured walk, run, or pull session before expecting calm thresholds — drain the tank deliberately.

**Use when:** Spitz or sled types destructive or vocal when under-exercised.

**Interrupts:** frustration reactive, frenetic arousal

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [access](#guide-training--access), [daily](#guide-daily-life--daily)

##### Run-then-settle cycles

Alternate vigorous outlet with enforced rest in crate or place — impulse control follows exhaustion, not lectures.

**Use when:** Cannot settle after insufficient physical work.

**Interrupts:** frenetic arousal

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [puppy daily structure](#daily-structure-awake-asleep-repeat), [access](#guide-training--access)

##### Fence and threshold management

Fences and gates matter — escape drive is real. Earned access beats repetition drills for recall.

**Use when:** Independent types bolt or fence-run when arousal builds.

**Interrupts:** barrier frustration

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [breed temperament](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application), [road safety](#road-safety-the-absolute-boundary-rural-nz)

#### Companion

**Earned proximity and check-in — not unlimited demand contact.**

**Fixation:** Velcro bonding, demand paw, and handler focus — contact sought as currency without structure.

##### Seven-second check-in games

Reward spontaneous glances every ~7 seconds during engagement — proactive conditioning, not panic.

**Use when:** Building pack awareness without anxiety-inducing hide tactics.

**Interrupts:** anxious attachment, fixation away from handler

**Life phases:** Puppy, Adolescent, Adult

**Guide sections:** [check in seven](#guide-daily-life--check-in-seven), [puppy check in](#the-seven-second-check-in--puppy-establishment)

##### Earned proximity vs demand lean

Calm four on floor or place earns contact; demand paw and lean at thresholds do not — see training vs living mode.

**Use when:** Small companion breeds negotiate for contact at every threshold.

**Interrupts:** anxious attachment, demand behaviours

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [context of contact](#the-context-of-contact-training-mode-vs-living-mode), [expectations](#guide-leadership--expectations)

##### Living-mode contact rules

Distinguish calm rest contact from training-mode accountability — warmth is not permission for demand behaviours.

**Use when:** Handler-attuned breeds blur rest and training boundaries.

**Interrupts:** handler-sensitive loops

**Life phases:** All

**Guide sections:** [context of contact](#the-context-of-contact-training-mode-vs-living-mode), [owner mindset](#guide-leadership--owner-mindset)

### Purpose roles

#### Trainer pack roles

##### Trick performer

A clicker-bright, handler-attuned dog that learns chains quickly and stays in the work without spinning into stress.

**For trainers:** Want high IQ, work, and adaptability with retrieve or herding-eye engagement. Giant frames and fear-reactive types make shaping a slog.

**For owners:** Best when the dog enjoys learning games, recovers fast after a miss, and does not shut down or explode under repetition.

**Preferred instincts:** Retrieve, Herding eye

**Tolerated instincts:** Companion, Scent

**Penalised instincts:** Guard, Chase

**Penalised stress patterns:** Fear reactive, Frenetic arousal, Frustration reactive

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Poodle (Standard) + ½ Border Collie:** Usable midpoint for tricks — Collie eye and Poodle trainability. Wide lottery on arousal: you may get a demo dog or a fixation loop.
- **½ Labrador Retriever + ½ Poodle (Standard):** Classic doodle gambit. Midpoint is cooperative and retrieve-bright; tails include handler-sensitive worry and coat/structure surprises.

##### Gold standard role model

The demo dog — calm, socially fluent, recovers to neutrality. Other dogs and humans read this one as the picture of the method.

**For trainers:** Prioritise emotional and social intelligence, low neuroticism, and adaptability. High dominance or frustration reactivity wrecks the model.

**For owners:** A dog that can hold a settle in public, greet without barging, and bounce back to calm after excitement — not a high-drive specialist.

**Preferred instincts:** Retrieve, Companion

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye

**Penalised instincts:** Guard, Hunt / dig, Chase

**Penalised stress patterns:** Frustration reactive, Fear reactive, Territorial vigilance, Frenetic arousal

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Aligned retrieve-and-people midpoint. Lottery is mostly energy and coat, not character — still not a guarantee of public neutrality.

##### Sentinel pack anchor

Settles a working pack by presence — socially fluent, stable nervous system, enough work ethic to hold a job without becoming the patrol.

**For trainers:** High social and emotional intelligence, moderate work, low neuroticism. Territorial vigilance as the primary job is guardian, not sentinel.

**For owners:** The dog other dogs orient to when the room gets noisy — calm, not a bouncer, not a velcro shadow.

**Preferred instincts:** Retrieve, Companion

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye, Guard

**Penalised instincts:** Hunt / dig, Chase

**Penalised stress patterns:** Territorial vigilance, Fear reactive, Frenetic arousal, Noise reactive

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Labrador Retriever + ½ German Shepherd:** Wide lottery — Labrador settle versus Shepherd patrol. Midpoint can be a superb pack anchor; the Shepherd tail is a guardian, not a sentinel.
- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Safer settle-and-social midpoint. Less presence than a Shepherd blend; more aligned nervous systems.

##### Emotional support dog for humans

A stable, people-oriented dog whose nervous system can co-regulate a human — not a needy mirror, and not a guard.

**For trainers:** High emotional intelligence and companion/retrieve drive with a genuinely stable nervous system. High protectiveness and fear-reactivity disqualify.

**For owners:** Warm, contact-tolerant, and recoverable — not a dog that panics at noise, patrols visitors, or collapses when you leave the room.

**Preferred instincts:** Companion, Retrieve

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye

**Penalised instincts:** Guard, Chase, Hunt / dig

**Penalised stress patterns:** Fear reactive, Noise reactive, Territorial vigilance, Hyper-vigilant, Frenetic arousal

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Aligned people-focus. The remaining lottery is energy and separation-sensitivity — structure still has to install the stable adult.
- **½ Cavalier King Charles Spaniel + ½ Miniature Poodle:** Small-frame ESD gambit. Midpoint is companion-bright; tails include anxious attachment and noise sensitivity if the Cavalier worry wins.

##### Helper dog: socialisation support

Models greeting, play, and recovery for client dogs — socially fluent, low reactivity, no guard rehearsal.

**For trainers:** High social intelligence, low neuroticism, retrieve or companion instinct. Guard drive and frustration reactivity turn “help” into a trigger.

**For owners:** The dog that makes other dogs look better — loose body, fair play, and a clean disengage. Not a corrector.

**Preferred instincts:** Retrieve, Companion

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye

**Penalised instincts:** Guard, Hunt / dig, Chase

**Penalised stress patterns:** Frustration reactive, Territorial vigilance, Fear reactive, Barrier frustration

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Aligned social midpoint. Individual dogs still vary in play style and adolescent rowdiness — select the adult, not the pedigree.

##### Helper dog: corrections and boundary enforcer

The master helper dog — enough presence and social intelligence to give native canine feedback without turning it into a fight.

**For trainers:** Need social intelligence, working drive, and enough dominance to hold a line. High protectiveness that becomes fight, or a fragile nervous system, disqualifies.

**For owners:** A balanced adult who can say “enough” to a pushy dog and then disengage — not a guard, not a bully, not a worrier.

**Preferred instincts:** Guard, Herding eye

**Tolerated instincts:** Retrieve

**Penalised instincts:** Chase, Hunt / dig

**Penalised stress patterns:** Fear reactive, Frenetic arousal, Noise reactive

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ German Shepherd + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Usable midpoint for a helper with presence. Shepherd tail can overshoot into guard/fight; Labrador tail can under-correct. Select the individual.
- **½ Rottweiler + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Wide lottery on dominance and protectiveness. The Labrador side can keep the Rottweiler from becoming a fight; it can also dilute the job.

##### Guardian

Directed protection and territorial assessment — guard instinct is the job, fear is not. Needs enough emotional intelligence to take direction.

**For trainers:** High protectiveness plus guard instinct, with enough EI to stay handler-directed. Fear-reactive and ESD-style cling both fail this role.

**For owners:** Alert and capable of holding a property or person — not a panic barker, and not a lap dog that happens to be large.

**Preferred instincts:** Guard

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye

**Penalised instincts:** Companion, Retrieve, Chase

**Required stress patterns:** Territorial vigilance

**Penalised stress patterns:** Fear reactive, Anxious attachment, Separation stress

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ German Shepherd + ½ Belgian Malinois:** Working-protection midpoint with a high-arousal Malinois tail. This is a specialist blend — not a family pet lottery you “hope settles”.

#### Family roles

##### Family active companion

A household dog with a real job in motion — runs, hikes, training games — whose drive has an outlet rather than becoming neurotic noise.

**For trainers:** Want working and instinct drive with enough EI to live in a house. High neuroticism is a caution, not always a disqualifier if the outlet is real.

**For owners:** Best when the household actually moves. A bored herding or hunting type in a quiet house is not “active companion” — it is a project.

**Preferred instincts:** Herding eye, Retrieve, Scent, Sled / endurance

**Tolerated instincts:** Hunt / dig, Companion

**Penalised instincts:** Guard

**Penalised stress patterns:** Fear reactive

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ NZ Heading Dog + ½ NZ Huntaway:** NZ farm midpoint — heading eye plus huntaway voice and stamina. Wide lottery on vocal output and eye-lock intensity. Needs land and a job.
- **½ Springer Spaniel + ½ Border Collie:** Known working-spaniel cross. Midpoint is motion-and-retrieve bright; Collie tail can be too much eye for a casual family.

##### Family low-active companion

A household dog that can live at a walk-and-settle pace — companion drive without a hunting or herding job that will go unused.

**For trainers:** Lower working and instinct scores, companion preference. High chase or hunt/dig will invent a job you did not ask for.

**For owners:** Fits a quieter home if structure is still real. Low-energy is not the same as no-training — manners still have to be installed.

**Preferred instincts:** Companion

**Tolerated instincts:** Retrieve

**Penalised instincts:** Chase, Hunt / dig, Herding eye, Guard, Sled / endurance

**Penalised stress patterns:** Frenetic arousal, Frustration reactive, Territorial vigilance

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Cavalier King Charles Spaniel + ½ Miniature Poodle:** Small companion midpoint. Poodle tail can raise work and noise; Cavalier tail can raise separation worry.

##### Family emotional anchor

The household’s calm centre — high emotional intelligence, people-focused, not a patrol, not a motion supervisor.

**For trainers:** High EI, companion/retrieve, low-to-moderate neuroticism. Hyper-vigilance and territorial vigilance fight this job.

**For owners:** A dog the family regulates around — contact-tolerant and recoverable — not an alarm system and not a herding nanny.

**Preferred instincts:** Companion, Retrieve

**Tolerated instincts:** Herding eye

**Penalised instincts:** Guard, Chase, Hunt / dig

**Penalised stress patterns:** Hyper-vigilant, Territorial vigilance, Fear reactive, Noise reactive

**Blend recipes:**

- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Labrador Retriever:** Aligned people-focus. Remaining lottery is energy: a high-octane Labrador is an active companion, not an anchor, until the adult settles.
- **½ Golden Retriever + ½ Poodle (Standard):** Groodle-style midpoint. Cooperative and people-bright; Poodle tail can add handler-sensitivity if structure is thin.

## Appendix E: Puppy Development

Developmental stages from birth to eighteen months, the nervous-system cultivation timeline, and sample daily plans at 8, 12, and 16 weeks.

### Stages at a glance

| Age | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| 0–8 weeks | With litter — safety baseline only (breeder) |
| 8 weeks – 4 months | Keep safe, build bond, potty training only |
| 4–7 months | Chew toys, tolerant dog play, no strict corrections |
| 7–12 months | Max exercise, heavy exposure, light enforcement late |
| 12–18 months | Strict accountability, solid recalls, no pulling/jumping |

### Development stages

#### Nesting phase (0–8 weeks)

**Core goal:** Foundational safety with mother, father, and littermates.

**Training intensity:** None

**Priorities:**

- Remain with the litter until ~8 weeks — early baseline of security
- Breeder handles weaning, bite inhibition with siblings, thermal co-regulation
- Not yet in your home — vet and breeder guide any intervention

**Defer:**

- Home potty training
- Formal obedience
- Leash corrections

#### Safety & routine (8 weeks – 4 months)

**Core goal:** Deep, unshakable feeling of safety — potty training is the overriding training goal.

**Training intensity:** Light

**Priorities:**

- Potty training above all other training goals
- Sleep close or in bed if needed for security (may complicate night toilet — worth the trade early)
- Light, low-pressure recalls — call over for treats; no enforcing methods yet
- Simple bond-building; chewing ramps at the tail end of this window

**Defer:**

- Standard leash corrections
- Strict obedience enforcement
- Hard accountability for blowing you off

#### Teething & satiation (4–7 months)

**Core goal:** Satiate the overwhelming urge to chew and mouth — they are temporarily out of their minds.

**Training intensity:** Light

**Priorities:**

- Immense focus on proper chew toys and approved textures
- Find at least one tolerant adult dog for safe jump, mouth, and wrestle play
- Walks and mental stimulation outside the home
- Patience when they pull, bark, or blow you off — brain is elsewhere

**Defer:**

- Hardcore leash corrections
- Forcing strict obedience rules
- Treating adolescent blow-off as defiance

#### Exercise, exposure & fear period (7–12 months)

**Core goal:** Navigate the adolescent fear period through purposeful exposure and high exercise.

**Training intensity:** Ramp up

**Priorities:**

- Drastically increase physical exercise and mental stimulation — adult-sized energy, teenage brain
- Active exposure during the fear period: hikes, markets, novel surfaces, swimming — do not over-shield
- Blowing you off at the dog park is normal at this age — not permanent attitude
- Toward 9–12 months: slowly introduce go-get recall and very light, tiny leash corrections

**Defer:**

- Full adult accountability standard until late in this stage
- Treating fear-period startle as permanent character

#### Accountability & serious training (12–18 months)

**Core goal:** Puppy passes are over — structured adulthood in a loving but firm way.

**Training intensity:** Full

**Priorities:**

- Clamp down on pulling, ignoring recalls, and jumping on people
- Solidify recalls and leash accountability
- Personality becomes fundamentally set around 18 months — coldness to other dogs at 9 months can become overt aggression by 18 months if unaddressed

### Nervous-system cultivation timeline

#### 7 weeks: Nesting phase

**What you observe:**

- Still with the litter — thermal co-regulation, sibling bite inhibition, and the first map of “the world is safe”.
- Nervous system is elastic and unfinished. Startle recovers fast if the nest is stable.

**Cultivate:**

- Breeder handling: short, calm, daily contact. Novel surfaces and household sounds at a distance — not flooding.
- Leave the pup with mother and littermates until ~8 weeks. Early baseline of security is the job.

**Defer:**

- Home arrival, formal obedience, and any correction that would be shocking in a finished adult.
- Isolating a 7-week pup “to bond with you” — that is a nervous-system injury, not training.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [puppy phase](#guide-puppy-phase--puppy-phase)

#### 8 weeks: Safety & routine

**What you observe:**

- Home arrival. Everything is new. The elastic nervous system will take its safety cue from the household, not from a sit.

**Cultivate:**

- Potty routine, sleep close if needed, and calm neutrality. Light recalls — call over for food; do not enforce.
- Voluntary contact is fine. Do not reward demanding paw or lean as the bonding ritual.

**Defer:**

- Standard leash corrections, strict obedience, and hard accountability for blowing you off.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [puppy phase](#guide-puppy-phase--puppy-phase)

#### 12 weeks: Safety & routine

**What you observe:**

- Peak socialisation window inside the safety-and-routine stage. Still a baby brain. Potty is still the overriding training goal.
- Elastic nervous system — firmness yes, shocking squeeze rarely. Capacity is short; recovery should be fast.

**Cultivate:**

- Broad, low-pressure exposure: surfaces, people, other stable dogs, car, vet handling. End while the body is still loose.
- Install “proximity is good” — guests arriving is not about the pup. Thresholds and crate/place as safety, not exile.

**Defer:**

- Hard corrections, leash pops as a system, and treating a blown recall as character.
- Drilling tricks or patrol rehearsal through this window — you will buy a stressed adult, not a specialist.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [puppy phase](#guide-puppy-phase--puppy-phase)

#### 4 months: Teething & satiation

**What you observe:**

- Teething and satiation. Temporarily out of their minds — mouthing, chewing, and blow-offs that are not attitude.

**Cultivate:**

- Chew toys and approved textures as the job. One tolerant adult dog for jump, mouth, and wrestle play if you can find one.
- Walks and mental work outside the home. Keep the safety baseline; do not moralise the mouth.

**Defer:**

- Hardcore leash corrections and forcing adult obedience while the brain is in the gums.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [puppy phase](#guide-puppy-phase--puppy-phase)

#### 7 months: Exercise, exposure & fear period

**What you observe:**

- Adolescent threshold — adult-sized energy, teenage brain. Testing, mounting, barging, selective deafness. Fear period often overlaps.
- Blow-off at the park is normal at this age — not permanent character.

**Cultivate:**

- Drastically increase exercise and novel exposure: hikes, markets, surfaces, swimming. Do not over-shield.
- Hold the adult standard from seven months for greetings and leash — excitement is not an excuse. Volume of the hand can rise; it is still not personal.

**Defer:**

- Full adult accountability until late in this stage. Treating fear-period startle as a permanent diagnosis.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [rehabilitation patterns](#guide-understanding--rehabilitation-patterns)

#### 12 months: Accountability & serious training

**What you observe:**

- Late fear-period / early accountability. Personality is setting. Coldness to other dogs at nine months can become overt aggression by eighteen if unaddressed.

**Cultivate:**

- Slowly introduce go-get recall and very light, tiny leash corrections. Clamp down on pulling and jumping as the months progress.
- Keep exposure active. Structure without flooding.

**Defer:**

- Waiting for them to “grow out of it” without a standard. Puppy passes are ending.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [rehabilitation patterns](#guide-understanding--rehabilitation-patterns)

#### 18 months: Accountability & serious training

**What you observe:**

- Personality is fundamentally set. Puppy passes are over. What you have been cultivating is now the adult nervous system.

**Cultivate:**

- Full accountability — recalls, leash, thresholds — in a loving but firm way. Rebuild quickly after a reset.
- Specialist jobs (helper, guardian, sentinel) are now selected from the adult in front of you, not the pedigree.

**Defer:**

- Starting a protection or helper-enforcer job on a still-fragile or still-fearful adult.

**Guide sections:** [breed age intensity](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks), [rehabilitation patterns](#guide-understanding--rehabilitation-patterns), [trauma hardship calibration](#calibrating-the-correction-scale)

### Cultivation by temperament type

Additional cultivation notes layered on the universal timeline for each temperament type.

#### Clingy & people-focused

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Bond forms fast — velcro and gaze arrive early.

**Cultivate:**

- Warmth with a frame. Access training starts as a game, not a freeze-out.

**Defer:**

- Face-gazing as the main bonding ritual; rewarding every whimper with a pickup.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Testing plus people-focus — pushy greetings look like love.

**Cultivate:**

- Hold the adult greeting standard. Excitement is not an excuse.

**Defer:**

- Negotiating with crying or guilt. That installs an emotional hostage, not an anchor.

#### Sighthound & chase type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Soft, easily startled. Calm at rest — then a flash of interest at motion.

**Cultivate:**

- Novelty gradually. Manage line-of-sight. Recover with neutrality, not drama.

**Defer:**

- Harsh correction that shuts them down. Off-lead near chase triggers.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Chase drive strengthens. One chase can rewrite the walk.

**Cultivate:**

- Line-of-sight management before off-lead access. Precursor window is the work.

**Defer:**

- Corrections aimed at a launched chase. Nothing outruns it.

#### Visual & herding type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Eye-lock and motion interest appear early — stare before the lunge.

**Cultivate:**

- Interrupt precursors. Short motion games with an off-switch. Avoid prolonged stare-and-pet.

**Defer:**

- Herding the children as cute. You are rehearsing the adult nanny-nip.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Fixation and arousal peak. Adolescent testing plus motion triggers.

**Cultivate:**

- Tighter timing, earlier interrupts, real jobs (flock, sport, structured fetch) instead of denied eye.

**Defer:**

- Hoping the stare “settles with age” while the household is the flock.

#### Spitz & sled type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Vocal, exploratory, independent. Recall is not a default.

**Cultivate:**

- Thresholds and fences as part of training. Earned access over repetition drills.

**Defer:**

- Hoping recall appears because you were fun at eight weeks.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Escape and frustration testing intensifies.

**Cultivate:**

- Structured outlets and earned access. Boredom is defiance fuel.

**Defer:**

- Nagging. They go independent on purpose.

#### Terrier & high-drive working type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Busy, mouthy, problem-solving. Boredom becomes yap and fixation quickly.

**Cultivate:**

- Channel dig, sniff, and puzzle drive daily. Access training is currency.

**Defer:**

- Lap-only raising with no job. Frustration will look like character later.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Frustration reactivity surfaces if outlets are thin.

**Cultivate:**

- Real jobs and earned access. Interrupt fixation early.

**Defer:**

- Repetition nagging. Terriers go deaf to lectures.

#### Scenthound & nose-led type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Nose comes online. Ears switch off when scent locks.

**Cultivate:**

- Recall before the nose locks. Food is usually currency. Baying is communication.

**Defer:**

- Moralising nose-led drift as defiance.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Trail commitment deepens.

**Cultivate:**

- Reserve high-value recall currency for off-lead windows. Sniff releases as decompression.

**Defer:**

- Heel battles against a locked nose as the only strategy.

#### Guardian & protection type

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Alertness appears early — wary glance at the door is already a seed.

**Cultivate:**

- Do not reward every wary glance with reassurance. Calm leadership from day one. Structured people exposure.

**Defer:**

- Patrol rehearsal, “protect mummy” talk, and isolation that confirms the world is unsafe.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Territory and stranger assessment sharpen.

**Cultivate:**

- Directed exposure — guests, trades, other dogs — with a handler who is not narrating threat.

**Defer:**

- Over-protection or complete isolation. Both grow a vigilante, not a guardian.

#### Giant & livestock guardian

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Habits cute at eight kilograms. Frame is already racing the brain.

**Cultivate:**

- Leash manners, thresholds, and calm greetings are non-negotiable now.

**Defer:**

- Carrying, indulging barge-ins, and “he does not know his size yet” as a plan.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Slow to mature — testing may run longer than smaller breeds. Size is already adult-dangerous.

**Cultivate:**

- Structure starts in puppyhood even if adult expectations apply later than two years.

**Defer:**

- Excusing size with weak structure. Privileged giants become entitled adults.

#### Small breed

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Easy to pick up. Pushy behaviour gets excused because they are cute.

**Cultivate:**

- Ground-level structure from the start. Same standard as a large dog.

**Defer:**

- Carrying, hand-feeding, and skipping thresholds because they fit under an arm.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Demanding behaviours peak if indulged early.

**Cultivate:**

- Adult standard from seven months. Touch saturation is a real risk.

**Defer:**

- Cute exceptions. Small dogs that cannot tolerate boundaries bite too.

### Cultivation by purpose role

#### Trick performer

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Curiosity and food interest — not a finished performer.

**Cultivate:**

- Short shaping games that end on a win. Name a settle as the off-switch.

**Defer:**

- Drilling chains through teething or a fear wobble.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Can learn fast and also spin out fast.

**Cultivate:**

- Keep sessions short. Reward recovery to neutrality, not just the trick.

**Defer:**

- Repetition until frustration. That is how you buy a frenetic demo.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult either recovers between reps or does not.

**Cultivate:**

- Select the individual for public work. Pedigree is not the act.

**Defer:**

- Pushing a still-brittle adult into a show schedule to “socialise them”.

#### Gold standard role model

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Social interest. Other dogs and people are the curriculum.

**Cultivate:**

- Calm greetings, loose body, and a settle that is boring on purpose.

**Defer:**

- Hyping them as the star of every room.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Adolescent rowdiness can look like the opposite of a model.

**Cultivate:**

- Hold the public settle. Fair play with other dogs. Instant disengage.

**Defer:**

- Letting them rehearse barge-and-mount as “just a teenager” without a line.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- This is the dog other dogs will copy — or avoid.

**Cultivate:**

- Protect the model. Do not use them as a punching bag for client dogs.

**Defer:**

- Burning out the best demo dog on every reactive intake.

#### Sentinel pack anchor

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Presence starts as calm-in-the-room, not patrol.

**Cultivate:**

- Other dogs in the home as background, not a job. Reward neutrality around movement.

**Defer:**

- Patrol rehearsal or “watch the pack” talk. That is guardian, not sentinel.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Can start to organise other dogs — or start to police them.

**Cultivate:**

- Reward settle while the pack moves. Interrupt stalking and body-blocks that are not asked for.

**Defer:**

- Letting them become the bouncer because it is convenient.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult either settles a room or runs it.

**Cultivate:**

- Keep the job as presence. If territorial vigilance won, re-home the job, not the standard.

**Defer:**

- Asking a vigilante to be the pack’s calm centre.

#### Emotional support dog for humans

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- People-focus is already there. Stability is not.

**Cultivate:**

- Co-regulation: handler calm, short absences that end well, noise at a distance.

**Defer:**

- Using the pup as a comfort object. That installs a needy mirror, not support.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Separation protest and noise startle show you the real nervous system.

**Cultivate:**

- Alone-time as a trained skill. Public neutrality. No patrol of visitors.

**Defer:**

- Emotional support “work” for a still-anxious adolescent. They cannot regulate you if they cannot regulate themselves.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- Stable or not is now visible.

**Cultivate:**

- Only then attach a human-support job. Select against fear and protectiveness.

**Defer:**

- Certifying a vigilante or a panic bark as an ESD because they like laps.

#### Helper dog: socialisation support

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Play interest. Bite inhibition still forming.

**Cultivate:**

- Fair play with stable dogs. Clean disengage. Loose body is the product.

**Defer:**

- Using them to “fix” reactive dogs. They are still a pup.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Can look like a helper and still rehearse rude play.

**Cultivate:**

- Reward the disengage. Interrupt pin-and-chase that client dogs will copy.

**Defer:**

- Helper work with bitey adolescents as the curriculum.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult either models recovery or models chaos.

**Cultivate:**

- Use only the fair, recoverable adult. Protect them from becoming a trigger.

**Defer:**

- A frustrated or guarding adult in the socialisation slot.

#### Helper dog: corrections and boundary enforcer

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Presence is not correction yet.

**Cultivate:**

- Social fluency first. They must be a fair dog before they are a line.

**Defer:**

- Encouraging puppy corrections of other dogs. You will grow a bully or a fight.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Enough size and enough test to overshoot.

**Cultivate:**

- Handler-directed interrupts. Reward disengage after “enough”.

**Defer:**

- Unsupervised dog-dog justice. Native feedback is not a free-for-all.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- This job is an adult selection.

**Cultivate:**

- Use only a stable, socially intelligent adult who can hold a line and then drop it.

**Defer:**

- A high-protection or high-neuro dog in the master-helper slot.

#### Guardian

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Alert seeds, not a finished guardian.

**Cultivate:**

- People as boring. Handler as the one who assesses. Exposure without reassurance-as-reward.

**Defer:**

- Protection sports, bite work, or “guard the house” games.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Territory sharpens. Fear period can look like protection.

**Cultivate:**

- Directed stranger work. Distinguish startle from assessment. Keep EI in the picture.

**Defer:**

- Confirming every bark. Isolation that grows a fear-biter with a job title.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult either takes direction or freelances.

**Cultivate:**

- Only then a protection job. Fear-reactive adults are not guardians.

**Defer:**

- Hoping a clingy or panicked adult “has your back”.

#### Family active companion

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Drive without an off-switch yet.

**Cultivate:**

- Daily motion that ends in a settle. Name the off-switch as clearly as the game.

**Defer:**

- All-day freedom with no job. That is how active types become neurotic noise.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Adult-sized energy. The household either moves or the furniture pays.

**Cultivate:**

- Hikes, training games, scent or flock as a real outlet. Hold greetings anyway.

**Defer:**

- A quiet-house plan for a heading dog. Change the dog or change the lifestyle.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult still needs a job. Age is not retirement at eighteen months.

**Cultivate:**

- Keep the outlet. Structure stays.

**Defer:**

- Dropping exercise because they “know better now”.

#### Family low-active companion

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- Can look easy. Manners still have to be installed.

**Cultivate:**

- Walk-and-settle rhythm. Same thresholds as a large dog.

**Defer:**

- Skipping training because they are “low energy”. Low-energy is not no-standard.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- If chase or hunt was hiding, it shows now.

**Cultivate:**

- Keep walks boring-on-purpose. Interrupt invented jobs (cat, shadow, yap).

**Defer:**

- Surprise agility careers for a dog you chose to be quiet.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult is either a settle companion or a frustrated under-worked mix.

**Cultivate:**

- Maintain the quiet job: walk, place, people as background.

**Defer:**

- Suddenly asking them to be a sport dog because a sibling got one.

#### Family emotional anchor

**12 weeks**

**Observe:**

- People-focus. Household emotion will become their weather.

**Cultivate:**

- Handler calm is the product. Contact without cling. Guests are not a crisis.

**Defer:**

- Using the pup to soothe family conflict. They will learn that distress is the job.

**7 months**

**Observe:**

- Can become the family barometer — or the family hostage.

**Cultivate:**

- Hold the standard through teenage noise. Alone-time. No patrol, no nanny-nip.

**Defer:**

- Dropping structure because they “know how you feel”.

**18 months**

**Observe:**

- The adult either regulates the room or the room regulates around their panic.

**Cultivate:**

- Protect the calm centre. Do not add guardian or herding jobs on top.

**Defer:**

- A hyper-vigilant adult as the household’s emotional support plan.

### Sample daily plans

*This planner is not veterinary advice. Confirm food amounts on your bag label and with your vet — especially if your puppy is underweight, vomiting, or lethargic.*

#### Puppy aged 8 weeks

**Development stage:** Safety & routine (8 weeks – 4 months). Deep, unshakable feeling of safety — potty training is the overriding training goal.

**Bladder hold:** about 3 hour(s), more often when active. **Awake block:** about 45 minutes. **Nap:** about 120 minutes.

| Time | Activity | Toilet trip | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7:00 AM | Wake — carry straight out; paws do not touch floor inside | Yes | Golden window: first thing on wake |
| 7:00 AM | Hand-feeding and short training — first third of daily ration |  |  |
| 7:15 AM | Short vigorous play, then wind down |  | Post-play toilet window is highest risk |
| 7:35 AM | Toilet trip — directly when play stops | Yes | Do not skip this transition |
| 7:35 AM | Crate or pen nap (~2 hr) |  | 18–20 hours sleep per day total |
| 9:35 AM | Wake from nap — immediate toilet trip | Yes |  |
| 9:35 AM | Low-arousal engagement on the ground — second third of ration |  |  |
| 9:50 AM | Short vigorous play, then wind down |  | Post-play toilet window is highest risk |
| 10:10 AM | Toilet trip — directly when play stops | Yes | Do not skip this transition |
| 10:10 AM | Crate or pen nap (~2 hr) |  | 18–20 hours sleep per day total |
| 12:10 PM | Wake from nap — immediate toilet trip | Yes |  |
| 12:10 PM | Training and play — final third of ration |  |  |
| 12:25 PM | Short vigorous play, then wind down |  | Post-play toilet window is highest risk |
| 12:45 PM | Toilet trip — directly when play stops | Yes | Do not skip this transition |
| 12:45 PM | Crate or pen nap (~2 hr) |  | 18–20 hours sleep per day total |
| 2:45 PM | Wake from nap — immediate toilet trip | Yes |  |
| 2:45 PM | Training and play — final third of ration |  |  |
| 3:00 PM | Calm play or chew — wind down |  | Post-play toilet window is highest risk |
| 3:20 PM | Toilet trip — directly when play stops | Yes | Do not skip this transition |
| 3:20 PM | Last-call toilet before bedtime crate | Yes |  |
| 3:20 PM | Bedtime — crate for the night |  |  |

**Early security:**

- Sleep close, warm, or in bed with you initially — mimic littermate security before standalone crate nights.
- Keep the puppy physically near you between naps — playpen, tether, or lap — not free roaming the house.

**Separation from the litter:**

- Separating from the litter at ~8 weeks is a real psychological hardship — loss of littermate co-regulation, not trauma in the damage sense.
- What may be missed: bite inhibition practice with siblings, thermal comfort of the pile, and learning to settle without constant contact.
- Early warmth is living-mode contact — see [the 8-week separation adjustment](#the-8-week-separation-adjustment). Structure still arrives; it arrives after safety is felt.

**Food and water:**

- Total daily amount: follow your food bag feeding guide for age and expected adult weight — confirm with your vet.
- Fresh water available at all times.
- Ensure the puppy receives enough total food per the bag — hunger training is optional; if not using food as currency, structured mealtimes still help toilet predictability.
- Typical rhythm: 3–4 smaller meals spread across waking blocks — aligned with your schedule table, not left in a bowl.

**Milk:**

- From 8 weeks home: solid puppy food per bag label. No cow milk. Weaning should be complete — vet check if appetite is poor.

**Track this week:**

- Sleep total (target ~18–20 hr/day at this age)
- Toilet successes and accidents — note post-play misses
- Appetite and stool quality
- Weekly weigh-in — compare trend to bag growth chart
- Mouthing intensity and overtired yap
- Check-ins during play — aim for glance every ~7 seconds when training
- Carry-out on wake still required? (paws off floor inside)

**Stage priorities:**

- Potty training above all other training goals
- Sleep close or in bed if needed for security (may complicate night toilet — worth the trade early)
- Light, low-pressure recalls — call over for treats; no enforcing methods yet
- Simple bond-building; chewing ramps at the tail end of this window

**Defer for now:**

- Standard leash corrections
- Strict obedience enforcement
- Hard accountability for blowing you off

**Bladder hold:** about 4 hour(s), more often when active. **Awake block:** about 45 minutes. **Nap:** about 120 minutes.

**Early security:**

- Transition toward crate independence now that the nervous system knows it landed somewhere safe — not before.

**Separation from the litter:**

- Sleep total (target ~18–20 hr/day at this age)

- Mouthing intensity and overtired yap

- Carry-out on wake still required? (paws off floor inside)

- Simple bond-building; chewing ramps at the tail end of this window

**Defer for now:**
