([guide](#surgical-alternatives-within-this-framework))

**Q77: (d)** That combination is not honest — intact life carries social penalty and a shrunk world unless you commit to a real path. Intact status shrinks the world and carries social friction. Choose Sentinel rigor, Containment management, or Socialite desexing with eyes open. ([guide](#the-critical-crossroads-three-lifestyle-paths))

### Road safety (7)

**Q78.** How does road safety differ from the controlled crucible used in off-lead social development?

- (a) Road safety uses the same fail-safely frame as off-lead playgroups — keeping the focus on gear rather than delivery
- (b) Traffic risk only matters for dogs under seven months old, before road sense develops on its own
- (c) Off-lead beside roads is fine once recall is solid in a paddock — yard success is trusted to transfer
- (d) Beside traffic there is zero tolerance — mistakes are fatal, not instructive; the reflex is built on-lead with no controlled failure

**Q79.** What is "semantic hijacking" in the car protocol?

- (a) Repurposing the existing word "Car" with a sharp, high-intent alert tone — same word, completely different psychological delivery
- (b) Inventing a brand-new traffic cue the dog has never heard before — looking harsh to onlookers is avoided even when a reset is needed
- (c) Saying "Car" louder each time until the dog holds still — so the standard rises only after more time has passed
- (d) Using the dog's name instead of a traffic-specific word — so the handler stays passive through the moment

**Q80.** An oncoming vehicle appears on a rural walk. What is the correct physical sequence after the high-intent "Car!" cue?

- (a) Sit on the pavement at the road edge and watch the car pass — leaving the pattern alone until it becomes urgent — acting after the full behaviour feels fairer because the dog has finished what it started
- (b) Immediate evacuation off the sealed edge → structured sit in the gutter or verge → hold still while tracking the passing vehicle → calm release only after it has fully passed
- (c) Recall across the road to the handler for safety — keeping the standard flexible for this dog — — so the outing stays pleasant for people nearby — repeating the cue is seen as patient teaching rather than renegotiating who decides
- (d) Lie down in the centre of the road so drivers can see the dog — because guests often encourage the same habit — the precursor looks polite from a distance, so people wait for a clearer full reaction

**Q81.** Why must the dog hold a stationary gutter sit while the vehicle passes?

- (a) Auditory tracking and immobility — the dog tolerates engine, tyre, and air pressure without drifting back toward the hazard
- (b) So passing drivers can see and photograph the trained dog — waiting for a clearer signal before stepping in
- (c) Because sitting on pavement is required by local traffic bylaws — because the dog already looks sorry enough
- (d) To practise a generic stay command that transfers to other settings — because the bond is prioritised over the rule

**Q82.** A dog hesitates at the pavement edge or breaks the gutter sit as a car approaches. How does the guide treat this?

- (a) A mild verbal reminder is enough beside traffic — keeping verbal tools only and avoiding contact
- (b) Ignore brief hesitation if the car is still far away — hoping the behaviour fades if it gets no audience
- (c) High-stakes failure — a definitive correction inside the one-second window; hesitation beside traffic is not everyday calibration
- (d) End all road training and avoid traffic outings from now on — food is expected to carry learning without access or structure

**Q83.** What does the "seven-month road crucible" mean?

- (a) At least seven months strictly on-lead while the car reflex is drilled, before off-lead access near roads is considered
- (b) Keep young puppies off all roads until they are at least seven months old and more mature — because one more chance is thought to teach patience
- (c) The same seven-month rule as adult I don't care expectations for behaviour at home — the bond is prioritised over the rule in hard moments
- (d) Seven months of soft reminders only — no firm corrections near traffic until the habit forms

**Q84.** When may off-leash freedom be granted within proximity of a rural roadway?

- (a) As soon as the dog is seven months old and knows sit, because age alone earns road freedom — a harness is chosen to avoid pressure on the neck during surges
- (b) Only after the on-lead car protocol is automated through months of repetition — a graduation decision, not a default from recall confidence elsewhere
- (c) Whenever the road looks quiet enough for judgment calls — trusting time and routine to smooth the edges — verbal tools alone are preferred to avoid physical contact
- (d) Keep them on-lead until you feel fully confident — there is no fixed graduation point — early interruption is thought to spoil play or social learning

#### Answers and explanations

**Q78: (d)** Beside traffic there is zero tolerance — mistakes are fatal, not instructive; the reflex is built on-lead with no controlled failure. Social crucibles allow controlled failure. Roadside, a boundary violation is not a learning opportunity — the standard is an invariant reflex drilled on-lead first. ([guide](#road-safety-the-absolute-boundary-rural-nz))

**Q79: (a)** Repurposing the existing word "Car" with a sharp, high-intent alert tone — same word, completely different psychological delivery. Most dogs already associate "Car" with outings. The protocol hijacks that familiarity — shifting delivery from casual invitation to non-negotiable alert. ([guide](#semantic-hijacking-repurposing-car))

**Q80: (b)** Immediate evacuation off the sealed edge → structured sit in the gutter or verge → hold still while tracking the passing vehicle → calm release only after it has fully passed. Cross the hard boundary onto earth or grass, anchor in a gutter sit, tolerate engine and tyre noise without breaking posture, release only when the threat is gone. ([guide](#the-car-protocol-alert-evacuate-anchor-release))

**Q81: (a)** Auditory tracking and immobility — the dog tolerates engine, tyre, and air pressure without drifting back toward the hazard. The anchor eliminates spatial drift. Holding still while the sound rises and falls teaches that car presence locks the body until the handler releases. ([guide](#the-car-protocol-alert-evacuate-anchor-release))

**Q82: (c)** High-stakes failure — a definitive correction inside the one-second window; hesitation beside traffic is not everyday calibration. On a normal walk, delay might earn a reset. Beside traffic, hesitation is systemic failure — corrections land with life-and-death intensity, then immediate calm release. ([guide](#road-safety-the-absolute-boundary-rural-nz))

**Q83: (a)** At least seven months strictly on-lead while the car reflex is drilled, before off-lead access near roads is considered. The road crucible is its own extended leashed runway. I don't care names adult behavioural rules; the gutter reflex must be muscle memory before freedom beside a roadway. ([guide](#the-seven-month-road-crucible))

**Q84: (b)** Only after the on-lead car protocol is automated through months of repetition — a graduation decision, not a default from recall confidence elsewhere. Recall in a paddock does not transfer to sealed edges. Off-lead near roads is earned only after the leashed crucible — hundreds of reps under mechanical control. ([guide](#the-seven-month-road-crucible))

### Corrections (17)

**Q85.** How does the guide define a correction?

- (a) A fast, calm interruption that redirects attention and resets the dog's body
- (b) A punishment that teaches the dog its behaviour was morally wrong
- (c) A consequence delivered after the outing, once you are home
- (d) Any expression of displeasure, including sighing and scolding — because exposure is thought to make reactivity worse

**Q86.** Why does yelling a dog's name during misbehaviour often fail to stop it?

- (a) Dogs are habituated to their owner's everyday voice and predictable touch — it no longer registers as an interruption
- (b) Dogs cannot hear their name when they are over-aroused — so the handler stays passive through the moment
- (c) Using the dog's name is wrong in every training context — because a single firm moment feels too severe
- (d) Dogs hear their name as a reward signal when excited — keeping the standard flexible for this dog

**Q87.** What is the core two-step pattern for stopping unwanted behaviour (as distinct from teaching commands like sit)?

- (a) A unique sound at the exact instant the behaviour starts, followed immediately by a unique touch
- (b) Repeat the command until the dog complies, then reward — because maturity is expected to fix the pattern
- (c) Wait until the behaviour finishes, then scold at home so the dog links the outing to the lecture
- (d) Use the same everyday voice with steadily increasing volume — because the walk should stay fun above all

**Q88.** Which two body locations does the guide name as the most communicative for the unique touch?

- (a) The flank (side) and the jawbone / base of neck
- (b) The top of the head and the tip of the tail
- (c) The chest and the front paws only, not the flank
- (d) The back and the belly — those areas feel more obvious to touch

**Q89.** A dog begins lifting a paw onto a table. When should the unique sound be delivered?

- (a) After all four paws are on the table and the behaviour is complete
- (b) Once you are home and can explain the mistake properly — because feedback is saved for when everyone is calmer
- (c) Only after the dog ignores a third verbal warning — because waiting feels fairer than interrupting the dog mid-choice
- (d) The exact millisecond the incorrect behaviour starts — as the paw begins to lift

**Q90.** Which of these is an effective unique sound for a correction?

- (a) The dog's name repeated louder with each repetition — keeping management light until a real problem shows
- (b) A sharp "Hey!", clap, or bark-like verbal pop — not the dog's name or a drawn-out scold
- (c) A long, soothing "Nooooo" so they hear your disapproval — so freedom is preserved as much as possible
- (d) Baby talk to calm them down without startling — so the dog feels comforted while the state is still active

**Q91.** Your dog is fixating and yap-barking in place at a trigger. Which tool is designed for exactly this?

- (a) The pin and hold until the dog goes still — other dogs are expected to teach manners without handler input
- (b) A treat lure to redirect attention away from the trigger — independence is read as dominance rather than breeding purpose
- (c) The butt push — a firm sideways push to the hindquarters that breaks the cycle
- (d) Pick the dog up and carry it past the trigger — the dog already looks sorry enough without further pressure

**Q92.** You have just delivered a butt push and the dog turned to you. What do you do next?

- (a) Watch closely to see whether the behaviour returns — because natural consequences are trusted to teach alone
- (b) Immediately return to calm, forward-facing posture and expect the dog to settle
- (c) Praise warmly so the dog knows the correction is over
- (d) Repeat the push once more to make sure the message landed

**Q93.** What is the correct direction and duration for a leash correction?

- (a) A steady upward pull held until the dog calms
- (b) Repeated small tugs in any direction until the dog responds
- (c) One firm downward jerk, then immediately back to slack
- (d) Sustained sideways tension to steer the dog away

**Q94.** What makes a verbal correction effective?

- (a) A long, drawn-out "Nooooo" so the dog hears your disapproval — noise is read as play and silence as safety
- (b) Repeating the word, raising the volume each time — because guests often encourage the same habit
- (c) A gentle, soothing tone so the dog does not get scared — because the dog already looks sorry enough without pressure
- (d) A single sharp "pop" of sound — bark-like, expelled in one instant, never repeated louder

**Q95.** Your dog jumps up at a visitor. What is the correction pattern?

- (a) Push the dog off with your knee and turn away — leaving natural consequences to do the teaching
- (b) Ask the visitor to ignore the dog until it stops jumping — the behaviour is expected to fade if it gets no audience
- (c) Grab the collar at the neckline, give a clear "No", walk the dog backwards, and sit them down
- (d) Pull the leash upward to lift the front paws off the person — leadership is expected to emerge naturally without claiming decisions

**Q96.** When is it appropriate for an owner to use the pin and hold at home?

- (a) Whenever lighter corrections have failed twice in one outing
- (b) Any time the dog growls at a family member in the house
- (c) Once the dog is over two years old and physically mature
- (d) Never without hands-on guidance — it is demonstrated in sessions only

**Q97.** How do you build a verbal correction so it can eventually replace the physical one?

- (a) Use the word on its own from day one — dogs learn words quickly — maturity is assumed to fix what structure has not yet addressed
- (b) Pair the word with the physical correction in the same instant, every time, until the sound alone breaks the behaviour
- (c) Use a different word each time so the dog generalises the concept — reassurance feels like leadership when the dog is already aroused and looking for support
- (d) Say the word after the physical correction as a closing marker so the dog knows the moment is over

**Q98.** Your dog jumps on you repeatedly when you arrive home. Which correction fits here?

- (a) Ignore until the dog calms on its own — jumping is just excitement and will fade with time
- (b) Collar grab and forced sit — interrupt the jump cycle, then settle before warmth returns
- (c) Step back and offer a treat for four paws down only, so the dog learns jumping loses rewards
- (d) Push the dog away gently each time without a full reset, so it learns you do not want contact

**Q99.** Your dog mouths your hand during play and you feel it escalating. How should you respond?

- (a) Let mouthing continue until the dog tires — puppies need to learn bite inhibition through natural play
- (b) It is not a game — interrupt with gruff correction or collar grab; play with rules, not endless tolerance
- (c) Redirect to a toy only and avoid correcting mouth contact on the handler, so play stays positive — because open space is thought to prevent real conflict
- (d) Yelp like a puppy to teach bite inhibition through social feedback, the way littermates would — because loose leads are thought to show trust and reduce tension

**Q100.** A confident adolescent dog tests boundaries daily with mounting and barging. How firm should correction be?

- (a) Softer than with a puppy because adolescents are emotionally fragile and need extra reassurance
- (b) No physical correction until three years old — wait for full maturity before holding a firm line
- (c) Maximum firmness first to establish leadership before any warmth returns for the rest of the day
- (d) Firmer line than with a soft puppy — still not personal, still instant release after the correction

**Q101.** An adult dog with shutdown history flinches at sudden movement. What approach fits?

- (a) Lighter entry and slower arc — structure without flooding; avoid shocking physical escalation early
- (b) The same firmness as a confident pushy adult from day one, so the dog learns the standard fast
- (c) Avoid all correction until trust is perfect, because any firm line will undo the bond you are building
- (d) Only verbal praise until six months of bonding, so the dog feels safe before any physical tools

#### Answers and explanations

**Q85: (a)** A fast, calm interruption that redirects attention and resets the dog's body. Corrections are not punishment in anger — they are fast, calm interruptions used inside the one-second window. The core mechanic is a unique sound followed immediately by a unique touch. ([guide](#guide-training--corrections))

**Q86: (a)** Dogs are habituated to their owner's everyday voice and predictable touch — it no longer registers as an interruption. Dogs habituate to familiar tone, repetitive words, and predictable touch. A unique sound at the exact instant of the behaviour snaps attention back — see Unique sound & touch. ([guide](#the-mechanic-unique-sound-then-unique-touch))

**Q87: (a)** A unique sound at the exact instant the behaviour starts, followed immediately by a unique touch. Teaching commands is repetition and reward. Stopping unwanted behaviour requires a unique sound plus unique touch — a stimulating boundary the dog has not learned to ignore. ([guide](#the-mechanic-unique-sound-then-unique-touch))

**Q88: (a)** The flank (side) and the jawbone / base of neck. The flank touch (butt push) breaks in-place reactivity; the jawbone/neck touch steers momentum away from triggers — collar grab & forced sit. ([guide](#the-mechanic-unique-sound-then-unique-touch))

**Q89: (d)** The exact millisecond the incorrect behaviour starts — as the paw begins to lift. The sound must land at the instant the behaviour begins — inside the one-second window. Delayed correction does not interrupt the live impulse. ([guide](#the-mechanic-unique-sound-then-unique-touch))

**Q90: (b)** A sharp "Hey!", clap, or bark-like verbal pop — not the dog's name or a drawn-out scold. The sound must be unique — a sharp interruption, not everyday voice. Pair with the touch in the same instant until the association is solid. ([guide](#guide-training--verbal-correction))

**Q91: (c)** The butt push — a firm sideways push to the hindquarters that breaks the cycle. The butt push is the primary tool for in-place reactivity — the continuous bark, the stare, the stiffening that feeds on itself. ([guide](#guide-training--butt-push))

**Q92: (b)** Immediately return to calm, forward-facing posture and expect the dog to settle. Immediately return to your calm posture. Don't hover or watch for what it does next — correct and move on, as if it barely warranted your notice. ([guide](#guide-training--butt-push))

**Q93: (c)** One firm downward jerk, then immediately back to slack. One sharp pull down, then back to slack. Never upward — that risks the larynx. Never sustained tension. ([guide](#guide-training--leash-jerk))

**Q94: (d)** A single sharp "pop" of sound — bark-like, expelled in one instant, never repeated louder. The command needs a pop — a single sharp release of sound that resembles a bark. If they ignore it, return to physical + verbal together; repeating the word louder trains ignoring. ([guide](#guide-training--verbal-correction))

**Q95: (c)** Grab the collar at the neckline, give a clear "No", walk the dog backwards, and sit them down. For behaviour that comes at you — jumping, lunging, mouthing — grab the collar, deliver the verbal, walk backwards to break momentum, then guide into a sit. ([guide](#guide-training--collar-snatch))

**Q96: (d)** Never without hands-on guidance — it is demonstrated in sessions only. Pin & hold sits at the top of the escalation ladder and is sessions-only. If nothing in the daily toolkit is landing, that is a session conversation — not something to improvise at home. ([guide](#guide-training--pin-hold))

**Q97: (b)** Pair the word with the physical correction in the same instant, every time, until the sound alone breaks the behaviour. The word must land in the same one-second window as the physical correction until the association is solid. When the dog visibly responds to the sound alone, test without the hands. ([guide](#guide-training--verbal-correction))

**Q98: (b)** Collar grab and forced sit — interrupt the jump cycle, then settle before warmth returns. Jumping up gets a collar grab and forced sit. You interrupt, reposition, settle, then rebuild calm contact on your terms. ([guide](#guide-training--jumping-up))

**Q99: (b)** It is not a game — interrupt with gruff correction or collar grab; play with rules, not endless tolerance. Mouthing that escalates is not play to indulge. Dog-language corrections are matter-of-fact — you set the rules. ([guide](#not-a-game--someone-has-to-be-the-boss))

**Q100: (d)** Firmer line than with a soft puppy — still not personal, still instant release after the correction. Adolescents test hard; the volume of the hand rises while the standard holds. Correct in the act; rebuild with calm neutrality. ([guide](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks))

**Q101: (a)** Lighter entry and slower arc — structure without flooding; avoid shocking physical escalation early. Shutdown history needs lighter entry and patience. The standard remains, but flooding confirms the world is unsafe. ([guide](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks))

### Leash work (4)

**Q102.** What does a constantly tight, upward-pulled leash communicate to the dog?

- (a) That you are nervous and reactive — creating a feedback loop of escalation
- (b) Clear leadership and control through constant tension — because the dog already looks sorry enough without pressure
- (c) Nothing — dogs only respond to voice commands on a walk
- (d) That the walk is nearly over and it is time to head home

**Q103.** Why is a slack leash described as "information"?

- (a) It tells the dog you have stopped paying attention to the walk — natural consequences are trusted to do the teaching alone
- (b) It signals to other owners that your dog is friendly and approachable — the dog park is trusted to socialise problems away
- (c) It lets you see who your dog actually is — where attention goes, how quickly it fixates
- (d) It reduces wear on the collar and lead over long outings — a vet check is assumed to explain the pattern first

**Q104.** Why does walking position matter — dog beside or slightly behind you?

- (a) It is purely about obedience competition rules and heel placement — waiting for a clearer signal before stepping in
- (b) Dogs behind you cannot see triggers and so cannot react — because the standard is kept flexible for this personality
- (c) It keeps the dog out of the way of other walkers on narrow paths — because the standard is kept flexible for this personality
- (d) A dog walking ahead concludes it is responsible for the pair — a burden that produces anxiety

**Q105.** Downward leash pressure is hard for you to apply — a small dog, or limited grip strength. What does the guide suggest?

- (a) Switch to a harness and pull backwards instead — keeping the focus on gear rather than delivery with this dog
- (b) Attach the leash to a short stick held against the ground, pulling the dog down without fighting upward tension
- (c) Use upward pressure — gentler and easier on a small dog — so the dog practises the skill only when ready
- (d) Skip physical corrections and rely on treats alone — so food alone is expected to carry the learning

#### Answers and explanations

**Q102: (a)** That you are nervous and reactive — creating a feedback loop of escalation. A tight leash tells the dog you're nervous. You tighten, the dog feels it and escalates, you tighten more. Sustained tension is anxiety transmitted through a leash. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q103: (c)** It lets you see who your dog actually is — where attention goes, how quickly it fixates. A relaxed leash lets you read the dog's personality and natural impulses rather than suppressing them with constant tension. You can't see any of that through a tight line. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q104: (d)** A dog walking ahead concludes it is responsible for the pair — a burden that produces anxiety. A dog that walks ahead has concluded it is responsible for the pair. Walking beside you means you're in charge of what's out there, and the dog can simply be a dog. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q105: (b)** Attach the leash to a short stick held against the ground, pulling the dog down without fighting upward tension. The stick assist: with the stick held against the ground, the dog is pulled down through the leash — making the downward jerk achievable and consistent. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

### Access & rewards (12)

**Q106.** In access training, what happens when behaviour falls short of the standard during off-leash time?

- (a) The dog gets a verbal warning and one more chance off-lead — toy scale is assumed to make real harm impossible
- (b) The leash goes back on with a tone of calm disappointment — that choice cost access
- (c) You end the walk and go straight home in silence — the precursor looks polite from a distance, so people wait
- (d) You withhold dinner that evening so the lesson lands overnight — companion breeds are assumed to need only love, not structure

**Q107.** You unclip the leash. What should the dog do?

- (a) Run immediately — freedom is the whole point of unclipping and should not be delayed
- (b) Sit for exactly seven seconds, then leave on their own — so daily handling stays easy without a clear cost with this dog
- (c) Stay within one metre of you for the rest of the outing — more intensity is assumed to equal more respect from the dog
- (d) Still wait — release from the leash is not release to run; they hold until you say go

**Q108.** If using treats, what kind works best as a reward signal?

- (a) Their favourite treat, given whenever they do anything good throughout the day — because maturity is expected to fix what structure has not
- (b) The dog's normal kibble, so rewards stay consistent with meals — because that path feels simpler in the moment with this dog
- (c) A rare, high-value treat the dog hasn't been overexposed to — like dried liver — kept training-only
- (d) Large treats, so the reward takes longer to eat and feels bigger — because guests and family often encourage the same habit

**Q109.** A dog ignores treats in training. What should you check before switching to a different reward?

- (a) Nothing — a dog that ignores treats is not food-motivated, so move straight to access rewards
- (b) Whether the treat is overused, the dog is hungry, and a favourite is reserved for training only
- (c) Withhold meals until food becomes motivating again, then resume treat training as usual — because acting after the behaviour feels fairer to the dog
- (d) Keep trying random new treats until one finally works, without changing hunger or session setup

**Q110.** Your dog shows no interest in food during sessions, yet eats dinner enthusiastically every night. What is the most likely explanation?

- (a) A setup problem — the training treat is overexposed, not reserved for sessions, or the dog isn't hungry at training time
- (b) The dog is genuinely not food-oriented and needs access rewards instead — keeping cooperation tied to snacks rather than access
- (c) The dog is unwell and should see a vet before training continues — ruling out health before any training pressure is added
- (d) The dog has learned that refusing treats earns more handler attention — because a better menu is thought to fix the gap

**Q111.** You train right after your dog has eaten its meal, and it ignores the treats. What has gone wrong?

- (a) The treats are too small to compete with a full meal — because food is expected to carry learning without structure
- (b) The dog isn't hungry — appetite is part of what the food reward depends on
- (c) Nothing — full dogs learn just as well as hungry ones — because food is expected to carry learning without structure
- (d) The dog is being stubborn and needs a firmer correction — because a stronger message is thought to land faster

**Q112.** Why should the dog's single favourite treat be reserved exclusively for training sessions?

- (a) So the dog doesn't gain weight from too many treats — so food alone is expected to carry the learning with this dog
- (b) Because favourite treats are usually expensive — keeping cooperation tied to snacks rather than access with this dog
- (c) To prevent other family members from confusing the dog with mixed cues at home — working drive is expected to fade with enough physical exercise
- (d) Rarity keeps it powerful — given freely, it stops being currency and loses its value as a reward signal

**Q113.** Why is saying "good boy" during or just after a reactive episode a mistake?

- (a) It is not a mistake — reassurance helps a stressed dog settle
- (b) Dogs find the phrase "good boy" overstimulating in any context — because the household wants peace first
- (c) It rewards the episode — praise must be saved for calm, correct behaviour
- (d) Verbal praise only works when paired with a treat — because reassurance feels like care during a spike

**Q114.** You give your dog's favourite treat throughout the day for minor behaviours. In training sessions, it ignores that same treat. Why?

- (a) The dog has developed an allergy to the treat — because a better menu is thought to fix the gap with this dog
- (b) You picked the wrong treat — switch to something higher value for sessions — repeating the cue is seen as patient teaching, not renegotiation
- (c) Training sessions are inherently less rewarding than daily life — because guests and family often encourage the same habit
- (d) Overuse has drained its value — rarity supports the process, so it must be reserved for training only

**Q115.** With treat setup ruled out, a dog still ignores food but pulls hard toward sniffing spots and fixates on movement. What currency should you train with?

- (a) A higher-value treat than the one currently used in sessions
- (b) Access and environmental rewards — earned off-leash time, sniffing, and running
- (c) Verbal praise delivered in an excited, high-energy tone only
- (d) Longer walks so the dog tires out and accepts treats again

**Q116.** A people-focused dog works hard for calm approval but shows little interest in treats. How should its reward currency be delivered?

- (a) As excited cuddling the moment the dog does anything right
- (b) As calm affection after correct behaviour — never during reactivity
- (c) Treats should still be forced as the primary reward for consistency
- (d) Approval should be withheld entirely so the dog works harder for it

**Q117.** You have ruled out the usual treat setup problems — the treat is not overused, the dog is hungry at training time, and a favourite is reserved for sessions only — but the dog still ignores food in training. What should you do next?

- (a) Repeat the diagnostic checks until food starts working — so food alone is expected to carry the learning on this outing
- (b) Identify what the dog actually wants — access, play, or social interaction — and use that as the currency
- (c) Train without rewards, since this dog cannot be motivated — because the handler wants peace more than clarity with this dog
- (d) Withhold meals so hunger eventually makes treats valuable — keeping cooperation tied to snacks rather than access on this outing

#### Answers and explanations

**Q106: (b)** The leash goes back on with a tone of calm disappointment — that choice cost access. Misbehaviour costs access: leash on, calm disappointed tone — not anger, not a lecture. The leash removes freedom, not as punishment but as neutral consequence. Clip on, reset, walk on without dwelling on it. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q107: (d)** Still wait — release from the leash is not release to run; they hold until you say go. Unclip — and the dog still waits. Release from the leash is not release to run. They hold until you tell them they can go. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q108: (c)** A rare, high-value treat the dog hasn't been overexposed to — like dried liver — kept training-only. Use a rare, high-value treat and reserve it for training sessions only. The rarer the treat, the stronger its value as a reward signal — handing it out through the day drains exactly the value training depends on. ([guide](#guide-training--rewards))

**Q109: (b)** Whether the treat is overused, the dog is hungry, and a favourite is reserved for training only. Ignoring treats is usually a setup problem, not a temperament verdict. Check overuse, hunger, and training-only reservation before switching currency. ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q110: (a)** A setup problem — the training treat is overexposed, not reserved for sessions, or the dog isn't hungry at training time. A dog that eats meals well clearly values food. Fix the setup first — rarity, reservation, and appetite — before concluding the temperament isn't food-oriented. ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q111: (b)** The dog isn't hungry — appetite is part of what the food reward depends on. Training straight after a meal, or with kibble available all day, removes the appetite the reward depends on. Check hunger as part of the treat diagnostic before changing anything else. ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q112: (d)** Rarity keeps it powerful — given freely, it stops being currency and loses its value as a reward signal. The ultimate treat must never be overused or it loses its value — the rarity supports the process. Reserve it for sessions: not walks, not settling, not "just because." ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q113: (c)** It rewards the episode — praise must be saved for calm, correct behaviour. "Good boy" during or just after a reactive episode rewards the episode. Save verbal praise for calm, correct behaviour — delivered calmly. ([guide](#guide-training--rewards))

**Q114: (d)** Overuse has drained its value — rarity supports the process, so it must be reserved for training only. This is the treat exploit being abused. The ultimate treat must never be overused or it loses its value — handed out casually, it stops being currency exactly when you need it in training. ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q115: (b)** Access and environmental rewards — earned off-leash time, sniffing, and running. Pulling toward sniffing and fixating on movement are signals of an access-oriented dog. Earned off-lead time, sniff, and run become the primary currency — the core of access training. ([guide](#reading-what-your-dog-actually-wants))

**Q116: (b)** As calm affection after correct behaviour — never during reactivity. Socially-oriented dogs respond strongly to calm approval. Deliver affection calmly after correct behaviour — excited delivery re-elevates energy, and affection during reactivity rewards the episode. ([guide](#reading-what-your-dog-actually-wants))

**Q117: (b)** Identify what the dog actually wants — access, play, or social interaction — and use that as the currency. Only after the setup checks are ruled out can you conclude the dog genuinely isn't food-oriented. Then read the orientation signals — access, play, or social — and match the motivator to the dog, not the other way around. ([guide](#reading-what-your-dog-actually-wants))

**Q118.** Roughly how long is the association window for a correction or reward to connect with a behaviour?

- (d) As long as the

**Q119.** You discover a chewed shoe from earlier in the day. What does correcting the dog now achieve?

- (a) Confusion — you are not interrupting a live impulse, so the correction teaches nothing
- (b) A delayed but still effective lesson, if you show the dog the chewed shoe
- (c) Reinforcement of your leadership, even without a live association — because a clearer signal is awaited before stepping in
- (d) Prevention — the dog will avoid shoes to avoid the correction — because exposure is thought to make reactivity worse

**Q120.** Why does the guide say to react to the precursor rather than the full behaviour?

- (b) Corrections during a full reaction are dangerous to the handler
- (c) Precursors last longer, giving you more time — because pressure feels unfair in the moment
- (d) It is easier to interrupt an impulse than a full reaction

**Q121.** You miss the one-second window. What now?

- (a) Correct anyway — better late than missing the chance entirely — late correction is still thought better than missing the moment
- (b) End the outing as a consequence for the missed window — because management feels safer than training through the moment
- (c) Let it go — stay calm, stay close, and be faster on the next moment
- (d) Recreate the situation so you can correct it properly — freedom is preserved as much as possible in daily life

#### Answers and explanations

**Q118: (a)** About one second. The response must land within roughly one second of the behaviour. Beyond that, the dog cannot reliably connect the two. ([guide](#guide-training--timing))

**Q119: (a)** Confusion — you are not interrupting a live impulse, so the correction teaches nothing. You are not punishing a memory; you are interrupting a live impulse. Delayed correction doesn't teach — it just confuses. ([guide](#guide-training--timing))

**Q120: (d)** It is easier to interrupt an impulse than a full reaction. Watch for the head snap, the body freeze, the first intake of breath before a bark. It's easier to interrupt an impulse than a full reaction. ([guide](#guide-training--timing))

**Q121: (c)** Let it go — stay calm, stay close, and be faster on the next moment. If you miss the moment, let it go — wait for the next one and be faster. Delayed correction doesn't teach. ([guide](#guide-training--timing))

#### Answers and explanations

**Q122: (c)** Back inside, sit, wait — then try again without drama. If they surge or push past, reset: back inside, sit, wait — then try again. Dogs that bolt through doors learn their impulse sets the pace for the whole walk. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q123: (a)** Every gateway — front door, car boot, yard gate. No door is a free pass. Same standard at every gateway. Calm wait before the leash goes on, before the door opens, before they step through. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q124: (d)** After release, a pack-minded dog should glance back your way within seven seconds. When you release the dog, count to seven. The glance back is the check-in: "I'm still with you; I'm still reading you." No glance — the access contract is broken, leash on. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--check-in-seven))

**Q125: (d)** Confident, resilient puppies only — never fearful, shutdown, or trauma-signalling dogs. Use the hide tactic only with confident, resilient puppies. For fearful or trauma-signalling dogs, shorten the distance and rebuild check-in at closer range instead. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--check-in-seven))

**Q126: (b)** A consistent ten minutes every day — more valuable than an occasional hour. Practice every day, even briefly. Use every walk as a training session until the behaviours are solid — not a separate "training walk" versus a casual one. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--daily))

**Q127: (b)** Mixed messages make the transition exponentially slower — the same rules apply regardless of who is present. The dog doesn't get exceptions for family members who haven't been trained yet. Mixed messages do not just slow progress — they make the transition exponentially slower. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--graduation))

**Q128: (d)** As a useful rule of thumb, not a deadline — consistency matters more than the calendar. Some dogs move faster; others need longer, especially with trauma, high reactivity, or inconsistent handling. Two households following the same method can look very different at the three-week mark. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--daily))

- (b) Unlimited pull-to-scent freedom — denying the nose is cruel — because the handler wants peace more than clarity at this stage — size is used as an excuse because the behaviour looks cute and guests often laugh
- (c) Only at the very start of the walk, then rigid heel for the rest — leaving the pattern alone until it becomes urgent at this stage
- (d) Structured earned access with frequent proactive thresholds — explicit sniff breaks are powerful currency, released on your cue and calibrated to the dog; pulling before release loses the break

**Q168.** Your scenthound freezes, head down, locked on a scent trail, about to launch. What is the correct response?

*Most relevant for Scenthound & nose-led type dogs.*

- (a) Interrupt now — this is the precursor window; the butt push or leash correction lands here, not after the trail takes over
- (b) Wait to see whether the dog chooses to leave the trail on its own first — because maturity is assumed to fix what structure has not
- (c) Call the recall repeatedly from a distance — so the outing stays pleasant for people nearby at this stage
- (d) Drag the dog away while soothing it — because the dog already looks sorry enough at this stage

**Q169.** Why are leash manners non-negotiable from day one with a giant breed puppy?

*Most relevant for Giant & livestock guardian dogs.*

- (a) Giant puppies are stronger than adult dogs of other breeds — trusting time and routine to smooth the edges at this stage
- (b) Habits cute at eight kilograms are dangerous at sixty — the standard must be set before the size arrives
- (c) They are not — giant breeds are too young to train before one year — because companion dogs are assumed to need only love
- (d) Because giant breeds cannot learn after six months, so early work is the only window — because early interruption is thought to spoil play or learning

**Q170.** Your giant or livestock guardian type ignores commands and patrols the property line instead. What is the correct reading?

*Most relevant for Giant & livestock guardian dogs.*

- (a) Independence by design — livestock guardians were bred to decide without instruction; structure must make compliance worthwhile, not assume biddability
- (b) Dominance that requires harsh confrontation until the dog submits and yields fully — exposure is thought to make reactivity worse, so hard moments are avoided for now
- (c) Deafness or a medical issue — vet check before any training — so training waits until a medical cause is cleared with this dog
- (d) Laziness typical of large breeds that will outgrow with age — so the handler stays passive through the moment at this stage

**Q171.** How does slow maturity change training expectations for a giant breed?

*Most relevant for Giant & livestock guardian dogs.*

- (a) It does not — all breeds mature at the same rate, so age rules are the same for everyone
- (b) Training should not start until maturity at three years — because maturity is expected to fix the pattern with this dog
- (c) Slow maturity means corrections are inappropriate — because a single firm moment feels too severe at this stage — because progress is kept visible without a hard reset
- (d) Adolescent testing arrives later and lasts longer — hold the same standard with patience; do not mistake a two-year-old for a finished adult

**Q172.** Your giant breed leans on visitors and pushes through doorways first. Why does this matter more than in a small dog?

*Most relevant for Giant & livestock guardian dogs.*

- (a) It does not matter more — size is irrelevant to structure — keeping the standard flexible for this dog at this stage
- (b) Giant breeds lean as affection and should be allowed — so the dog feels comforted while the state is still active on this outing
- (c) The same rank-testing is physically unmanageable at this size — thresholds and body-space rules are safety equipment, not etiquette
- (d) Because visitors might be allergic — ruling out health before any training pressure is added on this outing

**Q173.** A livestock guardian type barks at every passer-by from the yard. What does the guide-aligned response look like?

*Most relevant for Giant & livestock guardian dogs.*

- (a) Reassure the dog warmly each time so it feels safe — because reassurance is thought to calm the spike on this outing
- (b) Encourage it — guarding is what the breed is for — so freedom is preserved as much as possible at this stage
- (c) Butt push to interrupt the cycle; calm leadership and earned access so the dog stops running the watch alone
- (d) Leave it outside more so barking loses novelty — because guests often encourage the same habit at this stage

#### Answers and explanations

**Q129: (a)** Calm and matter-of-fact, never personal — these dogs are susceptible to emotional damage from harsh rejection. People-focused breeds bond intensely and can be damaged by corrections delivered with frustration or cold withdrawal. The tools still apply; the energy stays calm and matter-of-fact. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q130: (a)** Quickly — structure without warmth can read as abandonment to these dogs. Rebuild quickly after a reset — a quicker return to calm neutrality rather than prolonged coldness. Structure without warmth can read as abandonment. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q131: (a)** An emotional hostage dynamic — do not negotiate with crying or guilt; hold the standard with calm affection. Intense baby-style nurturing without boundaries makes the dog an emotional mirror. Warmth without structure is not kindness here — it is instability. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q132: (c)** Affection — delivered calmly, for calm and correct behaviour. These dogs can be highly responsive to affection as a reward. Match the motivator to the dog — and deliver it calmly, never during the excited state. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q133: (d)** It can blur the relationship frame and who leads the household — that is structure, not moral judgment. Allowing constant lap or bed access can blur the leadership frame and affect who leads the household rhythm. What you permit at home shapes what you get everywhere else. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q134: (d)** At the eye-lock — before the body moves; the precursor window matters even more for these dogs. Herding types may lock onto movement — eye contact can become a full fixation before the body moves. Watch for the eye-lock before the lunge. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q135: (b)** Movement-triggered herding instinct — interrupt at the precursor and channel outlets through structured access, not unstructured chasing games. Herding types are wired to track and intercept movement. Correct early, hold the standard calmly, and give earned outlets — not endless kid-chase as a substitute for structure. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q136: (b)** It can build attachment distortion — the dog treats you as an idealised, ever-present figure rather than a calm leader. A herding-type dog raised on face-to-face gazing may treat their person as something beyond ordinary. Leave the room and they may vocalise, refuse food, or look depressed — attachment distortion, not a medical mystery. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q137: (a)** Access training and environmental rewards, rather than treat-chasing. Access training and environmental rewards often land better than treat-chasing for dogs already wired to track motion. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q138: (d)** Likely attachment distortion — rebuild with structure, access training, and reduced face-gazing intimacy. It is often attachment distortion, not a medical mystery. Structure, access training, reduced face-gazing intimacy, and environmental outlets can rebuild a healthier frame. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q139: (b)** Frustration from denied outlets — sniffing, running, problem-solving — not bad character. Denying sniff, run, and problem-solving outlets builds frustration that surfaces as fixation, reactivity, or "naughty" destruction — not bad character. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q140: (c)** Access — off the leash, nose to the ground, free to run and sniff, on your terms. For dogs that are highly environmentally oriented, the reward isn't a treat or a pat. It's access: getting to be a dog, on your terms. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q141: (a)** Earned through trust, not default — behaviour directly controls how much freedom the dog has. Freedom is not their default. It is earned through trust, held briefly, and celebrated when given. When behaviour falls short, the leash goes back on. That is clarity, not cruelty. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q142: (a)** Outlets — sniff, run, and problem-solving time, structured as earned access. Frustration from denied outlets surfaces as fixation and reactivity. Access training is often the right currency for these dogs. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q143: (d)** The firmness and recovery time — same tools, calibrated to the dog in front of you. Age and temperament together set the floor: a soft adolescent and a hard adult may need the same technique with different firmness and recovery time. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q144: (a)** Entrenched anxiety — rewarding vigilance with reassurance teaches the dog its wariness is correct. Framing every wary glance as "protective love" and rewarding vigilance with constant reassurance can entrench anxiety. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q145: (b)** Calm leadership and earned access — more than comfort-talk. Calm leadership and earned access matter more than comfort-talk for guardian and alert breeds. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q146: (a)** An insecure leader is one the dog feels compelled to protect — it fills the leadership gap with guarding. If you're anxious, the dog becomes your guardian. If you're calm and certain, it relaxes into being your companion. Most "difficult" behaviour disappears when owner regulation improves. ([guide](#guide-leadership--owner-mindset))

**Q147: (a)** Correct at the precursor — butt push or downward leash jerk inside the one-second window, then calm forward posture. Stiffening is the precursor to reaction. Interrupt physically and calmly inside the window, then move on — reassurance during vigilance rewards the wrong state. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q148: (a)** Butt push to interrupt the cycle; calm leadership and earned access so vigilance is not the dog's job. The butt push is the primary tool for in-place reactivity — the continuous bark that feeds on itself. Long-term, calm leadership matters more than comfort-talk: a dog with a secure leader does not need to run the watch. ([guide](#guide-training--butt-push))

**Q149: (b)** A dog that cannot tolerate boundaries from anyone — including you. Carrying, hand-feeding, and excusing pushy behaviour because they are "cute" often produces a dog that cannot tolerate boundaries from anyone. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q150: (b)** Yes, fully — the standard is universal; only the delivery is calibrated to the dog's size. The structure in the guide is universal — every dog needs clarity, consistency, and a calm handler. What reads as a tap on one dog may be overwhelming on another; calibrate the delivery, not the standard. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q151: (b)** The stick assist — leash attached to a short stick held against the ground, pulling the dog down without upward tension. Bolt or attach the leash to a short stick. Held against the ground, the dog is pulled down through the leash — making the downward jerk achievable and consistent. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q152: (a)** Rank-testing that would be corrected in a big dog — the size excuse is teaching the dog that boundaries do not apply. Excusing pushy behaviour because the dog is "cute" produces a dog that cannot tolerate boundaries. The same standard applies: interrupt, reposition, settle. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q153: (b)** Learned dependency — over-sheltering from normal dog learning is harder to undo than to avoid. Constant carrying and over-sheltering from normal dog learning is one of the classic human-baby-trap pitfalls. Undoing learned dependency is slower and harder than building the right frame early. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q154: (b)** In the precursor window — the head-snap and body-lock before the launch; no correction outruns a chase already underway. Once a sighthound launches, the correction window has closed. Read the precursor — the visual lock and weight shift — and interrupt there, inside the one-second rule. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q155: (c)** Lighter entry — harsh delivery shuts these dogs down rather than teaching them; the standard holds, the volume drops. Age and breed together set the floor. Sighthounds are typically soft-tempered: the same technique applies with lighter delivery and quicker recovery — hold the standard, soften the drama. ([guide](#calibration-not-a-hard-rule))

**Q156: (c)** Yes — low energy at rest does not mean low need for leadership; the chase trigger is managed by structure built in calm moments. Sighthounds are calm, even lazy, at rest — then explosive on trigger. The structure built at doors, meals, and on leash in calm moments is exactly what holds when movement flashes. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q157: (c)** When it is earned and the environment is controlled — access is granted where the chase trigger can be managed, not hoped about. Access training applies: freedom is earned and granted where you can hold the contract. A fenced run area manages the trigger; an open field next to a road does not. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q158: (b)** Calmly — leash on, access ends, no anger at the return; punishing the come-back teaches the dog not to come back. Never punish the return — you would be correcting the recall, not the chase. The consequence is calm and structural: leash on, access lost, reset. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q159: (d)** Independence and boredom — repetition drills bore spitz types into defiance; earned access and varied outlets are the better currency. Spitz and sled types are independent by design. Endless repetition reads as pointless to them — structure the outcome they want (run, explore) as the earned reward instead. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q160: (c)** As part of the training picture from day one — thresholds, waits, and containment are core work, not an afterthought. Strong escape instincts are baked into the type. The front-door wait, gate manners, and earned access are the primary tools — and punishing a recovered escapee corrects the return, not the escape. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q161: (a)** Breed-typical vocal communication — hold the standard calmly; noise is not defiance or distress. Spitz types are famously vocal. Read it as information, hold the wait, and release on calm — rewarding the noise with release teaches the dog that volume opens doors. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q162: (b)** Structured, earned outlets — running, pulling work, long varied walks — destruction is unmet drive, not bad character. Endurance breeds were built to work for hours. Denied outlets, the drive surfaces as destruction or escape. The outlets are earned through structure — access training, not free-for-all. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q163: (a)** Earned in controlled environments with the seven-second check-in enforced — open-country freedom may never be appropriate for some individuals. The access contract is the same; the venue is chosen honestly. Some spitz individuals can earn open freedom, others hold it only in fenced spaces — read the dog, not the wish. ([guide](#guide-daily-life--check-in-seven))

**Q164: (c)** The nose has engaged and the ears have switched off — it is biology, not defiance; recall must be trained before the lock-on. When a scenthound's nose engages, recall fails on scent, not on respect. Interrupt in the precursor window — head dropping, tail rate changing — before the trail takes over. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q165: (c)** Food — most are strongly food-motivated, but the treat must be high-value and reserved for training or it loses to the scent. Most scenthounds are strongly food-driven, but an everyday snack cannot compete with a fresh trail. Run the treat diagnostic: rare, high-value, training-only. ([guide](#before-you-conclude-the-dog-isnt-food-motivated))

**Q166: (b)** As breed-typical communication — manage the arousal with structure, but do not treat the voice itself as naughtiness. Baying is how scenthounds communicate. Correct the behaviour you actually need changed — pulling, fixation — not the voice itself, and never reward the noise with excitement. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q167: (d)** Structured earned access with frequent proactive thresholds — explicit sniff breaks are powerful currency, released on your cue and calibrated to the dog; pulling before release loses the break. The nose is the dog's strongest drive — which makes sniff time powerful currency. Nose-led types often need more frequent, proactive release so heel stays coherent; the frame is still yours: earned breaks, your cue to end, no pulling into scent. See Sniff breaks. ([guide](#heel-earns-the-sniff-break))

**Q168: (a)** Interrupt now — this is the precursor window; the butt push or leash correction lands here, not after the trail takes over. The freeze-and-lock is the precursor. The one-second rule applies: act in the window before the nose fully engages, because after that the correction teaches nothing. ([guide](#guide-training--timing))

**Q169: (b)** Habits cute at eight kilograms are dangerous at sixty — the standard must be set before the size arrives. A jumping, pulling giant-breed adult is a safety problem no one can muscle through. Build the wait, the heel, and calm greetings while the dog is still small enough to correct easily. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q170: (a)** Independence by design — livestock guardians were bred to decide without instruction; structure must make compliance worthwhile, not assume biddability. Livestock guardian breeds were selected to work alone and make their own calls. They are not defiant — they are unconvinced. Earned access and consistent structure carry more weight than repetition. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q171: (d)** Adolescent testing arrives later and lasts longer — hold the same standard with patience; do not mistake a two-year-old for a finished adult. Giant breeds can be developmentally adolescent well past two. The standard holds throughout — but read rank-testing as developmental, correct it calmly, and expect the arc to be longer. ([guide](#age--temperament-how-hard-the-hand-speaks))

**Q172: (c)** The same rank-testing is physically unmanageable at this size — thresholds and body-space rules are safety equipment, not etiquette. Shoulder-barging and leaning are the same boundary tests every dog runs — but at sixty kilograms they knock people over. The front-door wait and butt push apply with full consistency. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q173: (c)** Butt push to interrupt the cycle; calm leadership and earned access so the dog stops running the watch alone. Guardian instinct plus no leadership equals a dog on permanent duty. Interrupt the rehearsal with a butt push, correct and move on — then build calm leadership so vigilance is not the dog's job. Save warm affirmation for earned calm, not during or just after the reactive episode. ([guide](#guide-training--butt-push))

### Body language (13)

**Q174.** A dog turns its head away from you but keeps watching — the whites of its eyes clearly visible. What does this usually mean?

- (a) Discomfort or conflict avoidance — the dog is stressed and not ready for interaction
- (b) Playfulness — because progress is kept visible without a hard reset — because handler guidance is seen as micromanagement socially
- (c) Dominance — the dog is challenging you and showing rank through the turned-away stare and tense body
- (d) Tiredness — the dog needs a nap and the whale eye is simply fatigue at the threshold

**Q175.** Your dog yawns at the front door when you arrive home, with no sign of tiredness. What is the most likely meaning?

- (a) The dog is bored and wants to go for a
- (b) The dog is hungry and wants dinner
- (c) The dog is relaxed and happy to see you
- (d) Displacement stress — tension release, not tiredness

**Q176.** A dog licks its lips repeatedly when no food is present and you have just leaned toward them. What does this signal?

- (a) The dog is hungry and wants a treat
- (b) The dog has tasted something on the floor
- (c) Appeasement or stress processing — the nervous system managing discomfort
- (d) The dog is about to bark playfully at you

**Q177.** As you reach to pet your dog, their body stiffens and weight shifts onto their back legs. What should you do?

- (a) Pet them anyway to show you mean no harm — because that path feels kinder day to day
- (b) Give a verbal correction for being unfriendly when you reach in
- (c) Offer a treat to change their mind — because life rewards feel too abstract compared with snacks
- (d) Create space — they are not ready for interaction; wait or approach differently

**Q178.** One dog approaches another with hackles raised and a stiff, silent body. What does this usually indicate?

- (a) Healthy excitement before a play bow starts up
- (b) Escalation precursor — real conflict risk, not healthy play
- (c) Submission — the dog is yielding space cleanly
- (d) Indifference — the dogs will ignore each other

**Q179.** A dog drops into a play bow — elbows down, rear up — but the body stays stiff and the stare is fixed. What does this mean?

- (a) Clear invitation to play — safe to engage when the elbows drop and the rear rises
- (b) Not a reliable play invitation — ambiguous; read tail, movement, and what happens next before engaging
- (c) Calming signal — appeasement shapes mean the dog is relaxed and ready — because open space is thought to prevent real conflict alone
- (d) Aggression — a stiff bow usually precedes a fight and needs immediate separation

**Q180.** After a tense greeting with a stranger, your dog does a full-body shake-off. What does this usually mean?

- (a) The dog is wet or uncomfortable from the collar
- (b) The dog wants to play with the stranger now
- (c) The dog is about to lunge and needs an instant correction
- (d) Stress reset — the dog marking that a moment has passed

**Q181.** Your adolescent dog repeatedly pushes past you through doorways and into your space shoulder-first. What is this behaviour?

- (a) Affection — the dog wants to stay close beside you now
- (b) Rank or momentum testing — information to correct early, not a personality flaw
- (c) Fear — the dog is trying to hide behind you for safety
- (d) Playfulness that should be encouraged — because the dog may only need more quiet reps

**Q182.** Your dog freezes, lowers its head slightly, and locks unblinking eye contact with you. What is this?

- (a) Play invitation — engage with rough wrestling to match the dog's energy and build bond
- (b) Soft check-in — the dog is asking permission before moving forward on the walk
- (c) A mean-mug challenge — rigid stare contest; break it with calm spatial pressure, not a stare-back battle
- (d) Medical concern — contact a vet urgently before any boundary correction continues in training today

**Q183.** Your dog holds a prolonged rigid stretch, tail down, staring at the wall. What is this most likely?

- (a) Medical emergency — prayer position; contact a vet urgently
- (b) A healthy greeting bow — safe to engage and play
- (c) Calming signal — the dog is relaxed and inviting contact
- (d) Dominance display — correct with spatial pressure immediately

**Q184.** Your dog shows whale eye as you reach to pet them. What should you do?

- (a) Pet anyway to show you mean no harm
- (b) Create space — do not scold or force interaction
- (c) Give a verbal correction for being unfriendly when you reach in
- (d) Laugh it off — sass is harmless and funny

**Q185.** The other dog in a meeting is braced, weight forward, and staring hard. What should you do first?

- (a) Increase distance and hold structure — do not close space while the other dog is in ready stance
- (b) Encourage a nose-to-nose greeting to break tension and show goodwill between the dogs — because noise is read as play and silence as safety
- (c) Reassure your dog with treats in the moment so it builds confidence near the other dog — because the dog looks distressed so comfort seems obvious
- (d) Turn your back so the dogs can sort it out without handler interference making things worse

**Q186.** Before a lunge, your dog freezes with weight forward and a hard stare at a trigger. What is this?

- (a) A sign the dog only needs more distance — no correction yet, because stillness means it is thinking
- (b) Play bow confusion — the dog is inviting interaction and will settle once contact starts
- (c) The dog's ready stance — read it early and intervene before the body commits
- (d) Dominance that requires you to stare back harder to reclaim leadership in the moment

#### Answers and explanations

**Q174: (a)** Discomfort or conflict avoidance — the dog is stressed and not ready for interaction. Whale eye — whites visible with head turned away — is a stress signal. Pair with stiff body or weight back before engaging. See Symptom glossary. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q175: (d)** Displacement stress — tension release, not tiredness. Yawning is displacement stress, not necessarily tiredness — often seen at thresholds: doorways, greetings, before a correction lands. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q176: (c)** Appeasement or stress processing — the nervous system managing discomfort. Lip licking is displacement or appeasement — nervous system processing stress. Watch what happened in the second before. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q177: (d)** Create space — they are not ready for interaction; wait or approach differently. Stiff posture with weight back means not ready for interaction. The three-second pause exists to catch this before you push through. ([guide](#the-three-second-pause))

**Q178: (b)** Escalation precursor — real conflict risk, not healthy play. Stiff approach with sustained hackles and silent hard staring are early conflict flags. See Dog meetings and Symptom glossary. ([guide](#when-dogs-meet-play-correction-and-real-conflict))

**Q179: (b)** Not a reliable play invitation — ambiguous; read tail, movement, and what happens next before engaging. The posture mimics a play bow, but stiffness and a fixed stare are not a safe play invite. The same shape can mean appeasement, stress, calming, or predatory arousal — context decides. A loose, bouncy bow is genuine play language. Do not assume play or that a fight is already underway. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q180: (d)** Stress reset — the dog marking that a moment has passed. Shake-off is reset after stress. Repeated shake-offs without settling may mean ongoing load. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q181: (b)** Rank or momentum testing — information to correct early, not a personality flaw. Shoulder barging tests rank or momentum. Treat as information and correct early — collar grab or butt push depending on the behaviour. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q182: (c)** A mean-mug challenge — rigid stare contest; break it with calm spatial pressure, not a stare-back battle. Rigid freeze plus hard locked stare is a rank challenge, not loose play. Break contact and hold the line. ([guide](#pushy-space-games-handler-directed))

**Q183: (a)** Medical emergency — prayer position; contact a vet urgently. A rigid front-down stretch held in place with stressed eyes is the prayer position — often severe abdominal pain or pancreatitis. Not a play bow. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q184: (b)** Create space — do not scold or force interaction. Whale eye is extreme anxiety, not sass. Forcing interaction validates panic and can trigger defensive bites. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q185: (a)** Increase distance and hold structure — do not close space while the other dog is in ready stance. A braced, staring dog is not ready for close contact. Read the other dog's ready stance and manage space before escalation. ([guide](#when-the-other-dog-is-braced))

**Q186: (c)** The dog's ready stance — read it early and intervene before the body commits. Braced weight forward and a hard stare is the dog's ready stance — the window before movement. You act before the body commits. ([guide](#reading-the-dogs-ready-stance))

### Relationship habits (10)

**Q187.** When you arrive home, your dog greets you with frantic helicopter tail-wagging and jumping. What does the guide recommend?

- (a) Match their energy immediately so they feel loved — waiting for a clearer signal before stepping in at this stage
- (b) Give a firm verbal correction each time it jumps at the door — because the dog may only need more quiet reps
- (c) Enter quietly, ignore for about sixty seconds, engage only after calm with four paws on the floor
- (d) Ignore the dog permanently — no greeting ever because many dogs grow out of the phase without pressure

**Q188.** Why does the guide recommend a three-second pause before petting or approaching your dog?

- (a) To make the dog wait as a dominance display — because dominance frames are still common advice
- (b) To read micro-signals — ears, eyes, weight — before pushing into an interaction they cannot comfortably exit
- (c) Because dogs cannot process touch for three seconds after movement — because the precursor looks polite so people wait to act
- (d) To build anticipation for a treat reward — so food alone is expected to carry the learning for now

**Q189.** Why is practising commands only in a quiet living room insufficient?

- (a) Dogs do not generalize easily — real progress happens when you reinforce spontaneous good choices in real environments
- (b) Living rooms are too small for proper training — because the bond is prioritised over the rule at this stage
- (c) Treats do not work indoors — keeping cooperation tied to snacks rather than access for now
- (d) Dogs cannot hear commands in quiet spaces — keeping verbal tools only and avoiding contact at this stage

**Q190.** Your dog does not sit on the first "sit" cue. What does the guide instruct?

- (a) Repeat the command calmly until the dog complies — patience teaches reliability better than pressure — the behaviour is expected to fade if it gets no audience and no further pressure
- (b) Check whether they heard, then at most one sharper repeat if fixation explains it; otherwise guide with body or leash — no third verbal cue
- (c) Assume defiance immediately and escalate to a pin and hold so the lesson lands hard — more intensity is assumed to equal more respect when the dog has already ignored a softer ask
- (d) Say sit a third time louder — three tries is the fair standard before any physical guide — anxious attention is read as care rather than insecurity the dog feels compelled to fix

**Q191.** Why must a command never be repeated a third time?

- (a) It validates boundary renegotiation and turns compliance into a game the dog can win — you end up being led
- (b) Dogs cannot process language after the second repetition, so more words only confuse them — because the dog mood is prioritised over holding the standard
- (c) The third repeat is when physical correction becomes illegal — so you reset later when everyone is calmer at this stage
- (d) It is only a problem for puppies under seven months, before adult focus develops — because energy is kept low until the dog offers calm

**Q192.** How should sniffing fit into a structured on-lead walk?

- (a) Heel earns sniff breaks on your release — grant short scent access when the dog needs to refocus; pulling before release costs the break
- (b) Ban sniffing on-lead entirely — it causes pulling and breaks heel, so the nose should wait until off-lead time — because the precursor looks polite so people wait to act
- (c) Let the dog pull to every scent — denying the nose is cruel and builds frustration that shows up at home
- (d) Hold rigid heel for a fixed distance, then allow one sniff at the end as the only reward for the whole walk — because energy is kept low until the dog offers calm

**Q193.** Your dog shows discomfort around a stranger reaching to pet them. What builds trust?

- (a) Encourage the stranger to keep petting so the dog learns people are safe — because other dogs are expected to teach manners alone
- (b) Pick the dog up and reassure them with baby talk — keeping connection first and structure second on this outing
- (c) Step in, create distance, and be a calm anchor — do not push them through for others
- (d) Leave immediately and avoid unfamiliar people until the dog matures — so the dog is left to choose without handler cost

**Q194.** Your dog nudges and squeezes until you move off the couch spot you were in. What is going on?

- (a) Displacing — claiming the resource; make them move, do not yield the seat
- (b) Cuddles — the dog wants closeness and you should shift over to make room
- (c) Anxiety — add reassurance and let them take the spot so they feel safe
- (d) Play — laugh it off and wrestle for the cushion to keep things light

**Q195.** Evening on the couch: loose body, your dog leans full weight against your legs. What should you do?

- (a) Push them off — all leaning is dependency and must be corrected
- (b) Pet immediately to reward the contact each time they lean
- (c) Accept it — living mode trust contact; do not push away
- (d) Stand up and practice heel position instead of resting

**Q196.** Your dog has constant lap access and sleeps on the bed every night. What does this mean for boundaries?

- (a) Bed access does not affect training if the dog is loved and bonded, because affection builds cooperation
- (b) Only large breeds need boundary rules at home — small dogs cannot challenge rank through lap access
- (c) Home boundaries are optional if walks are structured, because outdoor work covers the relationship frame — because tension on the lead is blamed for creating reactivity
- (d) What you permit at home shapes what you get everywhere — blurred access can affect rank and threshold behaviour

#### Answers and explanations

**Q187: (c)** Enter quietly, ignore for about sixty seconds, engage only after calm with four paws on the floor. Matching frantic greeting energy raises the arousal baseline. Wait for settled body before engaging — calm earns connection. ([guide](#coming-home-do-not-match-the-frenzy))

**Q188: (b)** To read micro-signals — ears, eyes, weight — before pushing into an interaction they cannot comfortably exit. The pause lets you read comfort level. Ignoring micro-signals leads to learned helplessness and behaviour owners call "snapping out of nowhere." ([guide](#the-three-second-pause))

**Q189: (a)** Dogs do not generalize easily — real progress happens when you reinforce spontaneous good choices in real environments. Carry reserved treats on real outings. Catch and reward spontaneous good choices — looking at you instead of a trigger, waiting without a prompt. ([guide](#guide-leadership--expectations))

**Q190: (b)** Check whether they heard, then at most one sharper repeat if fixation explains it; otherwise guide with body or leash — no third verbal cue. Learn your dog's heard-it signals. Fixation may warrant one escalated second cue; otherwise treat silence as renegotiation and guide physically. A third repeat validates the game and puts the dog in charge. ([guide](#1-say-it-once--hear-it-then-enforce-it))

**Q191: (a)** It validates boundary renegotiation and turns compliance into a game the dog can win — you end up being led. Two verbal attempts at most when fixation may explain the miss. A third repeat teaches the dog that holding out works — that is renegotiation, not training. ([guide](#1-say-it-once--hear-it-then-enforce-it))

**Q192: (a)** Heel earns sniff breaks on your release — grant short scent access when the dog needs to refocus; pulling before release costs the break. Scenting helps dogs decompress — not a prize withheld until exhaustion. You release on your cue; heel resumes on yours; pulling toward scent before release costs the break. ([guide](#heel-earns-the-sniff-break))

**Q193: (c)** Step in, create distance, and be a calm anchor — do not push them through for others. Trust is earned by advocating for the dog. Love without consistent advocacy does not build the trust reactive dogs need. ([guide](#trust-not-just-love))

**Q194: (a)** Displacing — claiming the resource; make them move, do not yield the seat. Couch takeover is displacing — a claim on the best seat. Yielding teaches pushy wins; reset position calmly. ([guide](#pushy-space-games-handler-directed))

**Q195: (c)** Accept it — living mode trust contact; do not push away. Voluntary lean during household calm is trust anchor contact in living mode — not the same as demand lean during training. ([guide](#the-context-of-contact-training-mode-vs-living-mode))

**Q196: (d)** What you permit at home shapes what you get everywhere — blurred access can affect rank and threshold behaviour. Household boundaries are structure, not moral judgment. Lap and bed access can blur the relationship frame this method depends on. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

### Equipment (8)

**Q197.** Which collar types does the guide prefer for pressure-and-release communication?

- (a) Chest harness with front clip for better control on pullers
- (b) Prong collar for strong pullers only
- (c) Flat collar or properly positioned slip lead
- (d) Heavy choke chain for instant control

**Q198.** Under what conditions might a head halter be appropriate in this methodology?

- (a) As the default collar for all reactive dogs from day one — because a harness is chosen to avoid neck pressure on surges
- (b) Whenever the dog pulls on walks — because the environment is blamed not the pattern at this stage
- (c) Only for puppies under six months, while they are still learning the house — because the household prioritises calm over clarity for now
- (d) Strictly as a temporary safety brake — extreme handler/dog size mismatch or severe handler physical limitation

**Q199.** Why does the guide exclude chest harnesses?

- (a) They are too expensive for most owners — assuming the dog will self-correct after one try at this stage
- (b) Dogs cannot sit while wearing a harness — keeping the focus on gear rather than delivery for now
- (c) They trigger the opposition reflex — encouraging the dog to pull harder against pressure on the chest
- (d) Harnesses only work on small breeds — so you only act when someone else is affected at this stage

**Q200.** Why are spiked / prong collars excluded from this methodology?

- (a) They are illegal in all countries — because the household prioritises calm over clarity for now
- (b) Sharp pain triggers fight-or-flight and closes the brain to calm, accountable learning
