- (c) Dogs become immune to prong pressure after one week of use
- (d) They only work on thick-coated breeds — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 135

**Q201.** Why are bungee leashes excluded?

- (a) They are too short for large breeds — so you build confidence before adding structure at this stage
- (b) Dogs are afraid of the bouncing sensation — because softer tools feel safer for the bond at this stage
- (c) Elastic delays pressure and release — the dog cannot learn the exact millisecond it made the correct choice
- (d) They prevent the handler from holding the leash at all — so control is lost by design

**Q202.** Why are extending / Flexi leashes excluded?

- (a) They are banned by local council bylaws everywhere — because the handler wants to avoid a scene
- (b) They maintain constant tension and teach the dog that pulling equals freedom
- (c) Dogs cannot smell properly on a long line — because calm matters more than clarity now
- (d) They only break in cold weather — because firmness alone is trusted to replace foundation work

**Q203.** What does a loose "U" shape in the leash between your hand and the dog's neck indicate?

- (a) The line weight is matched and the dog is regulating space — choosing cooperation on slack
- (b) The leash is too long and must be replaced — because a harness is chosen to avoid neck pressure on surges
- (c) The dog is about to bolt — leaving natural consequences to do the teaching at this stage
- (d) You are holding the leash incorrectly — keeping the focus on gear rather than delivery in this situation

**Q204.** When delivering a low-line corrective tug, where should your hand be positioned?

- (a) Above the dog's head for maximum leverage — because more intensity is assumed to equal more respect on this outing
- (b) Below the dog's neck line — angling pressure downward and sideways, not upward at the throat
- (c) At full arm extension behind you — so progress stays visible without a hard reset at this stage
- (d) Wrapped twice around your wrist for security — because the dog may only need more quiet reps at this stage

#### Answers and explanations

**Q197: (c)** Flat collar or properly positioned slip lead. Flat collar and properly used slip lead allow precise, instant pressure-and-release that teaches the dog to choose calm. ([guide](#guide-training--collar-selection))

**Q198: (d)** Strictly as a temporary safety brake — extreme handler/dog size mismatch or severe handler physical limitation. The head halter is never a core teaching tool — only a temporary management device for handler safety or breaking an explosive visual lock. ([guide](#when-the-head-halter-is-the-right-choice-coached-exception))

**Q199: (c)** They trigger the opposition reflex — encouraging the dog to pull harder against pressure on the chest. Chest harnesses wrap the strongest parts of the body and engage the opposition reflex — communicating pull, not cooperation. ([guide](#why-we-do-not-use-spiked-choker-or-chest--shoulder-harnesses))

**Q200: (b)** Sharp pain triggers fight-or-flight and closes the brain to calm, accountable learning. Pain spikes arousal and anxiety. A dog cannot learn accountability if its brain is wired shut by pain — see Collar selection. ([guide](#why-we-do-not-use-spiked-choker-or-chest--shoulder-harnesses))

**Q201: (c)** Elastic delays pressure and release — the dog cannot learn the exact millisecond it made the correct choice. Bungee leashes stretch before the dog feels pressure and snap back slowly after — muddying the pressure-and-release conversation. ([guide](#leash-selection-what-we-use-and-why))

**Q202: (b)** They maintain constant tension and teach the dog that pulling equals freedom. Extending leashes rely on spring tension — the dog must push forward to get line. That builds permanent pulling habits and eliminates handler control. ([guide](#leash-selection-what-we-use-and-why))

**Q203: (a)** The line weight is matched and the dog is regulating space — choosing cooperation on slack. The dangle is your dashboard — a properly weighted line loops in a U when the dog walks cooperatively on slack. ([guide](#line-weight-and-the-u-dangle))

**Q204: (b)** Below the dog's neck line — angling pressure downward and sideways, not upward at the throat. Low-line correction drops the hand below neck level — disrupting momentum without choking or triggering an upward pull reflex. ([guide](#biomechanical-handling))

### Adult expectations (6)

**Q205.** From roughly seven months onward, what does the "I don't care" rule mean?

- (a) The handler should ignore the dog entirely until it is two years old — because maturity is assumed to fix what structure has not
- (b) All corrections stop because the dog is now an adult — keeping energy low until the dog offers calm at this stage
- (c) The adult standard holds — nervousness and excitement do not excuse bolting, jumping, acting without permission, or walking ahead
- (d) Only fear-based behaviour gets a pass — excitement still requires structure — so daily handling stays easy without a clear cost for now

**Q206.** How does "I don't care" relate to "I'm over it"?

- (a) They mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably — because that path feels simpler in the moment for now
- (b) I'm over it is the attitude; I don't care is the adult standard that attitude enforces from seven months onward
- (c) I don't care replaces I'm over it once the dog is an adult — because onlookers shape how firm the handler is willing to be
- (d) I'm over it applies only to puppies — I don't care applies only to seniors — because onlookers shape how firm the handler is willing to be

**Q207.** An eight-month-old dog surges through the front door because it is "excited for the walk." What does the guide say?

- (a) Let it go — excitement at the door is normal for young dogs — because companion dogs are assumed to need only love
- (b) Only correct if someone is watching — private habits are thought not to matter — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 140
- (c) Reset — back inside, sit, wait. Excitement is not a reason to bolt; the I don't care standard applies
- (d) Switch to a harness so the surge does not hurt the neck — because verbal tools alone are preferred to physical contact

**Q208.** A nine-month-old dog jumps on visitors "because it is friendly." What is the guide-aligned response?

- (a) Allow jumping on people the dog knows well — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 141
- (b) Redirect with treats only — no physical correction after seven months — because a full reaction is easier to recognise than a lock-in
- (c) Hold the standard — four paws down or collar grab reset. Friendly excitement is not an excuse
- (d) Keep the dog in another room permanently — because the handler wants peace more than clarity for now

**Q209.** On a walk, an adult dog repeatedly cuts in front of you, pulling ahead with excitement. What does the guide expect?

- (a) Allow it — a happy dog should lead the walk — because management gear is treated as the primary solution
- (b) Switch to a Flexi leash for more freedom — more line is thought to reduce conflict on walks
- (c) Stop walking until the dog is over one year old — because a full reaction is easier to recognise than a lock-in
- (d) Reset position — the dog walks beside or slightly behind; excitement does not excuse surging ahead

**Q210.** On walks your dog leans its full weight into your leg to steer you off the path. What is this?

- (a) Trust lean in living mode — accept the contact and keep walking as the dog chooses
- (b) Fear — create distance and soothe until the dog relaxes before continuing the walk
- (c) Normal exploration — let the dog set the route so sniffing stays unrestrained
- (d) Displacing — claiming direction; reset position with leash work, not yielding the line

#### Answers and explanations

**Q205: (c)** The adult standard holds — nervousness and excitement do not excuse bolting, jumping, acting without permission, or walking ahead. I don't care is the adult standard I'm over it enforces. Past seven months, puppy excuses are closed — the line holds calmly. ([guide](#the-i-dont-care-rule--dogs-over-seven-months))

**Q206: (b)** I'm over it is the attitude; I don't care is the adult standard that attitude enforces from seven months onward. I'm over it is calm certainty that misbehaviour cannot win. I don't care names the non-negotiable adult rules that attitude protects. ([guide](#the-i-dont-care-rule--dogs-over-seven-months))

**Q207: (c)** Reset — back inside, sit, wait. Excitement is not a reason to bolt; the I don't care standard applies. No bolting through doors — wait, permission, then move. For dogs over seven months, nervous or excited is not an excuse. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q208: (c)** Hold the standard — four paws down or collar grab reset. Friendly excitement is not an excuse. No jumping on people — the I don't care rule applies. Compassion does not mean collapsing the standard. ([guide](#the-i-dont-care-rule--dogs-over-seven-months))

**Q209: (d)** Reset position — the dog walks beside or slightly behind; excitement does not excuse surging ahead. You lead. Cutting in front is not excused by excitement — see I don't care and Leash & line. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q210: (d)** Displacing — claiming direction; reset position with leash work, not yielding the line. Steer lean is displacing — the dog claims direction by making you move. Reset position; you lead the walk. ([guide](#pushy-space-games-handler-directed))

### Trainer calibration (10)

**Q211.** A privileged Labrador counter-surfs daily with no trauma history. Which driver fits best?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Trauma and security-first — lower all correction intensity
- (b) Entitlement and hardship — intentional boundaries, not trauma-soft handling
- (c) Neuro stress loop — open the substitution playbook first
- (d) Social dominance — rank navigation with other dogs

**Q212.** Handler-lick vs self-lick decoupling: when is a scheduled lickmat appropriate?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) At a dedicated calm time — never immediately after a human-licking episode
- (b) Immediately after the dog licks your hand, to redirect onto the mat
- (c) Only when the dog is actively licking your face, as instant redirection
- (d) Whenever the dog seems anxious, including mid-episode on your skin

**Q213.** An insecure Golden Retriever licks your hands; No and Stop make him sad and lick more. Best first move?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Repeat Stop firmly until the licking extinguishes — so early pressure is postponed on purpose with this dog
- (b) Offer a mouth job — Hold or soft toy — and build Chin for calm contact
- (c) Give a lickmat immediately after each lick episode to redirect — because one more chance is thought to teach patience on both sides
- (d) Ignore all licking until it stops on its own without guidance — because one more chance is thought to teach patience

**Q214.** Which pattern row is primarily hardship path, not substitution?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Anxious attachment — mouth job and Chin/Nose
- (b) Handler-sensitive — neutral baseline and decoupling
- (c) Fear reactive — security-first small wins at distance
- (d) Barrier frustration — leash accountability primary

**Q215.** A 14-month-old mounts other dogs at the park with a confident body. First driver to consider?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Age and development — adolescent testing; firm non-personal structure
- (b) Trauma security-first — no corrections at all yet
- (c) Handler-sensitive neuro loop — substitution only for now
- (d) Skill gap — basic sit not yet reliable at home

**Q216.** A Beagle trails scent and ignores recall. Before calling it a fixation neuro loop, consider?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Entitlement hardship — firm collar grab each time the head drops on trail
- (b) Separation stress — the dog is distressed when alone — because this feels kinder for the household 33
- (c) Breed expression — scent biology; train recall before nose locks, reserved high-value treat
- (d) Social dominance — rank issue with other dogs — because the pattern is not treated as urgent yet

**Q217.** Handler matches greeting excitement and the dog velcro-licks. Which driver do you fix first?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Neuro stress loop — start with Chin and mouth job immediately
- (b) Social dominance — dog-dog rank navigation — so the handler answers with rank instead of clarity
- (c) Skill gap — door manners not yet trained before any greetings
- (d) Owner dynamics — reset baseline and neutral home return before opening the playbook

**Q218.** How do you split pushy adult mouthing from insecure compulsive licking?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Both need the same Stop command until the behaviour extinguishes — because repeating the cue is seen as patient teaching
- (b) Pushy mouthing escalates when challenged — hardship; soft-body lick worsens under No — substitution
- (c) Both are dominance — stare down and collar grab — because management gear is treated as the primary solution
- (d) Both are trauma — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 159

**Q219.** Persistent paw licking with reddened skin. What must happen before a behavioural plan alone?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) Medical rule-out — allergy, hot spot, or pain — vet check
- (b) Immediate lickmat after every paw lick to redirect the habit
- (c) Verbal correction until the licking stops — because this feels kinder for the household 34
- (d) Ignore — all self-lick is anxiety and will fade with time

**Q220.** Distress vocalising when left alone vs velcro following room to room. These differ how?

*Trainer level.*

- (a) They are the same problem and need identical treatment in every case
- (b) Both are social dominance with other dogs — because noise is read as play and silence as safety
- (c) Separation is alone-time panic; velcro is handler-present anxious attachment — different pattern rows
- (d) Both mean the dog needs more lap access at home daily

#### Answers and explanations

**Q211: (b)** Entitlement and hardship — intentional boundaries, not trauma-soft handling. Pampered, entitled dogs need intentional hardship. Misreading as traumatised keeps bad behaviour alive — see driver calibration. ([guide](#behavior-driver-calibration))

**Q212: (a)** At a dedicated calm time — never immediately after a human-licking episode. Handler-targeted lick keeps human skin out of the reward loop. Self-lick may use scheduled outlet when calm — plus medical rule-out if hotspots present. ([guide](#compulsive-licking-of-handler))

**Q213: (b)** Offer a mouth job — Hold or soft toy — and build Chin for calm contact. Functional substitution over suppression — retriever genetic leverage plus proactive Chin/Nose nomination. ([guide](#1-functional-substitution-over-suppression))

**Q214: (d)** Barrier frustration — leash accountability primary. Barrier frustration: substitution alone fails; leash accountability and collar choice for frustration entitlement. ([guide](#barrier-frustration-1))

**Q215: (a)** Age and development — adolescent testing; firm non-personal structure. Adolescent mounting spikes with developmental testing. Still correct early — but read age before pathologizing as trauma. ([guide](#behavior-driver-calibration))

**Q216: (c)** Breed expression — scent biology; train recall before nose locks, reserved high-value treat. Failed recall on scent is often biology not defiance. Breed expression lens first; fixation loop if locked loop cannot break. ([guide](#behavior-driver-calibration))

**Q217: (d)** Owner dynamics — reset baseline and neutral home return before opening the playbook. Layering: owner dynamics amplifying anxious\_attachment. Fix handler contribution before substitution playbook. ([guide](#behavior-driver-calibration))

**Q218: (b)** Pushy mouthing escalates when challenged — hardship; soft-body lick worsens under No — substitution. Entitlement hardship vs anxious\_attachment substitution — driver calibration before tool choice. ([guide](#compulsive-licking-of-handler))

**Q219: (a)** Medical rule-out — allergy, hot spot, or pain — vet check. Self-target symptoms carry medical rule-out. Scheduled behavioural outlet only after health is cleared. ([guide](#compulsive-self-licking))

**Q220: (c)** Separation is alone-time panic; velcro is handler-present anxious attachment — different pattern rows. Separation pattern row vs anxious\_attachment symptom variants — identify target and pattern before playbook. ([guide](#separation-stress-1))

### Breed trait (35)

**Q221.** You have a Miniature Poodle. Your frustrated shouting during a reaction seems to make the dog more animated. What is happening?

*Most relevant for breeds: Miniature Poodle.*

- (a) The dog is dominant and needs harsher shouting to match the energy and win the argument
- (b) Ignore all reactions until the dog gives up — attention feeds the behaviour, so silence is the fix
- (c) Puzzle-driven types may read handler frustration as an interactive game — stay calm and matter-of-fact
- (d) Only food rewards work for intelligent breeds — shouting has no role and should be dropped entirely

**Q222.** You have a Toy Poodle. Guests laugh when it snaps because it is tiny. What should you do?

*Most relevant for breeds: Toy Poodle.*

- (a) Allow it for now — at this size the snap is more cute than dangerous, and guests usually enjoy the moment
- (b) Carry the dog away without correction to avoid stress, because tiny dogs cannot handle firm boundaries
- (c) Hold the same boundary standard as for a large dog — size excuses teach rank-testing that will not stay cute
- (d) Only correct when someone complains — otherwise let guests enjoy the greeting and keep the mood light

**Q223.** You have a Cavoodle. The dog whines when left and you soothe with baby talk. What is the risk?

*Most relevant for breeds: Cavoodle / Spoodle.*

- (a) Stress-sensitive crosses can spiral when distress is rewarded in the moment — structure and earned calm instead
- (b) Soothing builds security for companion crosses — keep reassuring until the dog calms and feels safe
- (c) Separation whining means the dog needs more lap time and closeness so it trusts you will return
- (d) Only crate training can fix this — structure at the door is irrelevant if the dog sleeps alone at night

**Q224.** You have a Golden Retriever. After a correction, how should recovery look?

*Most relevant for breeds: Golden Retriever.*

- (a) Cold withdrawal for ten minutes so the lesson lands and the dog has time to think about what it did
- (b) Skip correction and use treats only for this people-focused type, because firm tools damage the bond
- (c) Calm matter-of-fact reset, then rebuild warmth quickly — they tolerate recovery well when delivery is fair
- (d) Extra firmness because retrievers ignore soft tools and need a stronger message to respect you

**Q225.** You have a Standard Poodle. Mental work keeps slipping because walks are only physical. What is missing?

*Most relevant for breeds: Poodle (Standard).*

- (a) Channel puzzle drive into structured tasks and access training — mental work is not optional for this type
- (b) More fetch until tired — physical exhaustion replaces mental structure and keeps the dog settled at home
- (c) Puzzle drive fades after eighteen months — wait it out and the need for mental work will drop on its own
- (d) Only agility classes can satisfy this breed — home structure is not enough for a working mind

**Q226.** You have a Border Collie. It locks eye contact on a moving cyclist before the lunge. When should you act?

*Most relevant for breeds: Border Collie.*

- (a) Only when the feet leave the ground — wait for the full lunge so the correction is clear and fair
- (b) At the eye-lock precursor — before the body commits; access and environmental rewards often beat treat-chasing
- (c) After three seconds of staring to let the dog think through the trigger and choose to look away
- (d) Do not correct stare — it is natural herding and should be allowed as healthy breed expression

**Q227.** You have a Border Collie. You enjoy long mutual staring sessions on the couch. What pitfall applies?

*Most relevant for breeds: Border Collie.*

- (a) Long staring can intensify fixation and clingy focus on you — soften eye rituals at home
- (b) Longer eye contact deepens bond for herding breeds — lean into gazing sessions as daily connection
- (c) Only strangers should avoid eye contact — owner gaze is different and builds trust without risk
- (d) Staring is dominance and requires you to look away first to submit and keep the dog calm

**Q228.** You have a Staffy. You correct jumping, then stay cold for an hour. What went wrong?

*Most relevant for breeds: Staffordshire Bull Terrier (Staffy).*

- (a) Structure without warmth can read as abandonment — rebuild calmly after the reset
- (b) Staffies need longer cold periods than other breeds to respect the correction and remember it
- (c) Clingy breeds should not be corrected — corrections damage the bond these dogs need most
- (d) Only verbal tools work for staffy-types — physical reset is too harsh for a people-focused dog

**Q229.** You have a Staffy. It becomes the household emotional centre and you avoid any firm line. What fits?

*Most relevant for breeds: Staffordshire Bull Terrier (Staffy).*

- (a) Avoid corrections entirely because the bond is special for this breed and firmness would break it
- (b) Hold the standard with calm delivery — affection is currency, not a substitute for structure
- (c) Use only excited praise so the dog feels loved after every mistake and stays emotionally secure
- (d) Rehome if firmness is needed — this breed cannot handle structure and will shut down under rules

**Q230.** You have a Newfoundland. Visitors excuse jumping because it is a "gentle giant." What should you do?

*Most relevant for breeds: Newfoundland.*

- (a) Giant breeds should be allowed to lean for affection — that is their nature and guests expect it
- (b) Gentle temperament does not excuse thresholds — jumping cute at thirty kilograms is dangerous at sixty
- (c) Wait until full size before teaching door manners, so the dog is mature enough to understand waits
- (d) Only leash corrections work on giants — verbal cues are not enough when mass is this large

**Q231.** You have a Belgian Malinois. You feel anxious on walks and the dog spins up with you. What must change first?

*Most relevant for breeds: Belgian Malinois.*

- (a) Handler calm certainty — hyper-alert working types mirror anxious energy and need job-like structure daily
- (b) A firmer leash and prong only — tools before handler calm, because equipment fixes drive on its own
- (c) More off-lead time to burn energy and reduce anxiety, so the dog can self-settle without pressure
- (d) Avoid triggers until the dog matures at four years, when working drive naturally levels out

**Q232.** You have a Belgian Malinois with no daily structured work. What is the likely outcome?

*Most relevant for breeds: Belgian Malinois.*

- (a) Idle high-drive guardians become anxious and vocal — build job-like outlets or reactivity follows
- (b) They settle naturally in suburban homes without structured work once the honeymoon phase ends
- (c) Only agility competitors need daily structure — pet homes are fine with walks and free yard time
- (d) Mental toys alone replace training sessions, so puzzle feeders cover the need for handler-led work

**Q233.** You have a Labradoodle. Recall is fine but impulse control fails at thresholds. What fits this cross?

*Most relevant for breeds: Labradoodle / Groodle.*

- (a) Treat-only training because doodles are soft and sensitive, so physical tools would damage the bond
- (b) Assume retriever stability means no structure needed at thresholds — recall proves the dog is ready
- (c) Blend retriever cooperativity with poodle mental work — access training and structured tasks, not just exercise
- (d) Wait for maturity before any correction at doorways, because young doodles need freedom to settle

**Q234.** You have a NZ Huntaway. It barks at movement in the yard all day. What is the reading?

*Most relevant for breeds: NZ Huntaway.*

- (a) Barking is breed-appropriate and should be encouraged as expression so the dog does not bottle stress
- (b) Only citronella collars stop vocal breeds effectively, because training alone cannot override bark drive
- (c) Vocal working engine needs job-like outlets — interrupt rehearsal and build calm leadership, not endless patrol
- (d) Ignore barking so the dog learns it does not work, and the habit will fade without any interruption

**Q235.** You have a NZ Heading Dog. It stares silently at children running. What should you watch for?

*Most relevant for breeds: NZ Heading Dog.*

- (a) Stillness means the dog is calm and can be left to watch, because quiet dogs are not about to move
- (b) Quiet eye-lock before movement — precursor window is critical; intervene before the gather instinct commits
- (c) Only vocal dogs need precursor reads — silent stare is fine and shows the dog is thinking, not reacting
- (d) Herding stare should be rewarded as focus and engagement, so the dog learns looking is a good job

**Q236.** Your puzzle-driven dog pauses on-lead to look at a distraction, body still loose. What do you do?

*Most relevant for profile: puzzle driven.*

- (a) Correct every glance immediately to keep focus on the handler and stop looking away from you
- (b) Drop treats to refocus before the dog can look back at you, so food wins over the distraction
- (c) Shorten the walk whenever distraction appears — avoid the trigger entirely until the dog is older
- (d) Allow a brief self-regulation beat — tighten the line only if fixation locks in

**Q237.** Your intelligent, puzzle-driven dog seems to escalate when you shout during reactions. Why?

*Most relevant for profile: puzzle driven.*

- (a) The dog is testing dominance and needs a louder correction to match the energy and win the moment
- (b) Intelligent dogs only respond to food — voice has no training value and should be dropped entirely
- (c) Shouting works if you are loud enough to startle the dog and interrupt the reaction in one go
- (d) Owner frustration can read as an interactive challenge — calm matter-of-fact delivery is mandatory

**Q238.** Your stress-sensitive dog reacts at the door and you soothe with baby talk. What should you do instead?

*Most relevant for profile: neurotic, anxious.*

- (a) Increase soothing until the dog relaxes — comfort is the priority and builds long-term security
- (b) Remove all visitors until the dog is older and more settled, so stress has no chance to build
- (c) Hold structure — reward earned calm after reset, not soothing during the reaction
- (d) Only medication can change door reactions at this level, so training structure will not help yet

**Q239.** Your dog panics when left alone. What else matters alongside gradual absence work?

*Most relevant for profile: separation stress.*

- (a) Stay home until the dog is fully cured before any absence training, so panic does not have to happen
- (b) Consistent household structure and boundaries — not unlimited comfort that blurs rank and thresholds
- (c) Get a second dog immediately for companionship, because loneliness is the only driver of the panic
- (d) Ignore all distress until it stops — no comfort during panic, and no structure changes at home either

**Q240.** Your very small dog needs a downward leash correction but your hand position is awkward. What helps?

*Most relevant for sizes: toy, small.*

- (a) Lift by the harness instead — upward tension replaces the downward jerk and is gentler on a small frame
- (b) Stick assist — leash to a short stick on the ground for a consistent downward jerk without upward tension
- (c) Skip leash corrections under eight kilograms — too small for physical tools, so use voice and treats only
- (d) Use a heavier leash for leverage on a light dog, so the correction lands harder with less hand effort

**Q241.** You have a giant-breed adolescent who leans through doorways first. Why is this urgent?

*Most relevant for sizes: giant.*

- (a) Giants lean from affection and should be welcomed at doorways, because that is how they greet people
- (b) Wait until eighteen months to teach door waits — puppies need freedom before rules feel fair
- (c) The same rank test is physically unmanageable at full size — thresholds are safety equipment now
- (d) Only prong collars work on giants — verbal waits are not realistic when mass is this large

**Q242.** Your dog shows stress-looping when you comfort it during reactive episodes. What should you change?

*Most relevant for stress sensitivity elevated or higher.*

- (a) Comfort more intensely until the dog feels safe — reassurance is the fix and builds long-term trust
- (b) Reward earned calm after structured reset — comforting during the episode often feeds the loop
- (c) Avoid all training until the dog is calm for a full week, so stress has time to settle on its own
- (d) Only use crates for stress-looping dogs — no other structure needed once the dog is contained

**Q243.** Your toy-scale dog is treated as fragile and excused from every boundary. What fits?

*Most relevant for stress sensitivity high or higher.*

- (a) Fragile dogs need no correction — structure would break trust and make stress worse over time
- (b) Same standard, calibrated delivery — indulgence spirals are especially common at toy scale
- (c) Only positive reinforcement for toy breeds — no physical tools, because small dogs cannot handle them
- (d) Keep the dog indoors to avoid stress triggers entirely, so boundaries do not have to be tested

**Q244.** Your high-drive dog self-assigns work in the yard (digging, patrolling, fixating). What is missing?

*Most relevant for profile: high drive.*

- (a) More free time in the yard to burn energy naturally, so the dog settles without handler pressure
- (b) Only longer walks fix drive — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 179
- (c) Drive fades after neutering — wait for hormonal change and the self-assigned work will stop
- (d) Structured outlets and handler-led work — idle drive becomes rehearsal without a job frame

**Q245.** Your people-focused dog melts down when you correct and you avoid firmness to protect the bond. What should you do?

*Most relevant for profile: clingy.*

- (a) Deliver calm matter-of-fact correction, then rebuild warmth — structure without affection reads as abandonment
- (b) Skip correction for bonded dogs — the relationship is too important to risk with any firm line
- (c) Use only excited praise after mistakes to restore the bond, so the dog does not feel rejected
- (d) Send the dog away for an hour after every correction to let it think and respect the lesson

**Q246.** Your clingy breed paws forcefully at you during quiet time at home. What is this?

*Most relevant for profile: attention demand.*

- (a) Affection seeking that should be indulged on the couch, because clingy breeds need constant contact
- (b) A medical paw injury — stop training and see a vet before any boundary work continues
- (c) Attention demand — withhold engagement until calm; do not reward the paw cycle
- (d) Play invitation — engage right away to build the bond and meet the dog's need for interaction

**Q247.** Your guardian-type dog follows you to the bathroom and sits facing away. How should you read this?

*Most relevant for profile: pack guarding.*

- (a) Separation anxiety that needs soothing and extra reassurance whenever the dog follows you
- (b) Pack guarding instinct — protecting a vulnerable pack member, not pure annoyance
- (c) Dominance — the dog is claiming bathroom territory and must be blocked from entering
- (d) A habit to interrupt with spatial corrections whenever it happens, so the dog stops following you

**Q248.** Your 45 kg dog is entering physical prime. Why is the ready stance non-negotiable?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant.*

- (a) Large dogs only need verbal cues because they are calmer than small breeds and less likely to lunge
- (b) At this mass you cannot out-muscle a committed lunge — engaged core and stance are safety, not polish
- (c) Ready stance is optional once recall is reliable in the backyard, because obedience covers street risk
- (d) Harnesses provide enough control that handler stance does not matter once the dog is on a short lead

**Q249.** Your two-year-old large dog is still excused at thresholds because he feels young. What should shift?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant.*

- (a) Puppy mindset in you must end — project certainty; the standard starts at the door, not on the walk
- (b) Wait until four years when all large breeds are fully mature before holding boundaries at home — because time and routine are trusted to smooth the edges
- (c) Lower standards until he stops testing — he is still a puppy emotionally and needs more freedom
- (d) Use only treats at thresholds because physical corrections are unfair at two years of age — because the handler stays out of the social exchange on purpose

**Q250.** Your 47 kg intact male bolts through the front door ahead of you. Where should leadership have been established?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant; intact dogs; males; owners building structure.*

- (a) On the walk once he has burned energy — doors do not matter if recall is good later
- (b) Only after he has had a long run so he is tired enough to listen at the door
- (c) At the threshold before permission — eye contact and calm body verified before the door opens
- (d) At the park — home thresholds are separate from outdoor training and can stay casual

**Q251.** Your large intact male ignores recall on a walk and you chase with excitement. What does the guide expect?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant; intact dogs; males; owners building structure.*

- (a) Stop chasing — any pursuit teaches him running is fun, so wait until he chooses to return
- (b) Call louder and use a higher pitch until he feels how worried you are and comes back to help
- (c) Stop and recall from a distance — chasing any bolting dog rewards the game and makes it worse
- (d) Recall failure is not a game — pursue joylessly and relentlessly without drama he can feed on

**Q252.** Your large intact male demands a run by pulling and vocalising. When should the long run happen?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant; intact dogs; males; owners building structure.*

- (a) After calm coordination and focus are shown — access to runs and sniffs is your reward, not his demand
- (b) Immediately — tire him out first so pulling on the way is less of a problem and he settles faster
- (c) Only on weekends when you have more patience for pulling and can wait out the demand behaviour — because this feels like the kinder everyday choice 185
- (d) After neutering — drive for runs fades once hormones are removed, so wait for that change

**Q253.** An unfamiliar intact dog approaches for an unstructured off-lead greeting. What should you do?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant; intact dogs; males; owners building structure.*

- (a) Let them sort rank off-lead — intact males need to learn from other dogs without handler interference
- (b) Avoid all dog contact until he is neutered, because intact meetings are too risky to manage at all
- (c) Trust the greeting because the other dog looks friendly and wagging, so a free meet should be fine
- (d) Keep structure — leash, space, and earned calm before close contact; do not assume the other handler will manage

**Q254.** On lead, your large intact male locks eyes on another dog and his body braces forward. When should you act?

*Most relevant for sizes: large, giant; intact dogs; males; owners building structure.*

- (a) At the precursor — before the body fully commits; break visual lock and redirect while you still have leverage
- (b) Wait until he lunges so the correction is unmistakable and he clearly knows what he did wrong
- (c) Drop slack and let him approach to build social confidence, because tension on the lead creates reactivity
- (d) Only act if the other dog reacts first — your dog may settle if the other dog stays calm

**Q255.** An anxious, fearful dog is being considered for neutering. What does the guide warn?

- (a) Neutering usually removes fear because hormones were the main driver of the anxious behaviour
- (b) Removing testosterone can worsen baseline fear-reactivity or shyness rather than fixing it
- (c) Anxious dogs need softer structure only after desexing is complete, so wait before any firm line
- (d) Fearful dogs must be neutered immediately before any training begins, or progress will not hold

#### Answers and explanations

**Q221: (c)** Puzzle-driven types may read handler frustration as an interactive game — stay calm and matter-of-fact. Poodle-family puzzle drive can turn owner frustration into a game. Calm delivery and structured access beat escalating drama. ([guide](#guide-understanding--distraction-processing))

**Q222: (c)** Hold the same boundary standard as for a large dog — size excuses teach rank-testing that will not stay cute. Toy scale intensifies indulgence pitfalls. The standard is universal; you calibrate delivery to size, not the rule. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q223: (a)** Stress-sensitive crosses can spiral when distress is rewarded in the moment — structure and earned calm instead. Cavoodle-type crosses inherit miniature-poodle stress sensitivity. Reward earned calm, not the episode. ([guide](#love-at-the-right-time))

**Q224: (c)** Calm matter-of-fact reset, then rebuild warmth quickly — they tolerate recovery well when delivery is fair. Golden Retriever–stable types bond intensely but recover well from fair, calm correction. Rebuild warmth after the reset. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q225: (a)** Channel puzzle drive into structured tasks and access training — mental work is not optional for this type. Standard Poodles carry puzzle and problem-solving drive. Access, earned tasks, and structure land better than endless reps. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q226: (b)** At the eye-lock precursor — before the body commits; access and environmental rewards often beat treat-chasing. Visual herding types fixate before they move. The precursor window is the eye-lock — intervene early with calm tools. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q227: (a)** Long staring can intensify fixation and clingy focus on you — soften eye rituals at home. Collies and similar types can lock onto visual input — including long owner staring. Soften those rituals at home. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q228: (a)** Structure without warmth can read as abandonment — rebuild calmly after the reset. People-focused breeds need calm matter-of-fact correction, then a quick rebuild. Cold withdrawal damages these dogs. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q229: (b)** Hold the standard with calm delivery — affection is currency, not a substitute for structure. Staffy-types bond intensely but still need clarity and consistent boundaries. Delivery stays calm, never personal. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q230: (b)** Gentle temperament does not excuse thresholds — jumping cute at thirty kilograms is dangerous at sixty. Newfoundland-type gentleness is not permission to skip structure. Build waits and calm greetings while size is still manageable. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q231: (a)** Handler calm certainty — hyper-alert working types mirror anxious energy and need job-like structure daily. Malinois-types shut down or spin up with anxious handlers. Calm leadership and structured outlets are mandatory. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q232: (a)** Idle high-drive guardians become anxious and vocal — build job-like outlets or reactivity follows. Belgian Malinois carry among the highest working drive. Without daily structured outlets, reactivity and vocal stress follow. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q233: (c)** Blend retriever cooperativity with poodle mental work — access training and structured tasks, not just exercise. Labradoodle crosses vary — plan for puzzle drive and people-focus. Mental work and access both matter; you set the frame. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q234: (c)** Vocal working engine needs job-like outlets — interrupt rehearsal and build calm leadership, not endless patrol. Huntaways were bred to bark and move stock. Idle suburban life needs structured outlets and consistent interruption of rehearsal. ([guide](#guide-training--butt-push))

**Q235: (b)** Quiet eye-lock before movement — precursor window is critical; intervene before the gather instinct commits. Heading dogs gather with eye — silent stare at motion is a precursor, not calm. Read early and manage access. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q236: (d)** Allow a brief self-regulation beat — tighten the line only if fixation locks in. Puzzle-driven types often benefit from a slightly longer processing window when the body stays loose. You step in when fixation locks. ([guide](#guide-understanding--distraction-processing))

**Q237: (d)** Owner frustration can read as an interactive challenge — calm matter-of-fact delivery is mandatory. Handler-attuned puzzle types may gamify emotional drama. Stay calm and use structured tools — you set the tone. ([guide](#guide-understanding--distraction-processing))

**Q238: (c)** Hold structure — reward earned calm after reset, not soothing during the reaction. Soothing during reactions can reinforce stress loops. Structure, timing, and earned calm beat emotional rescue. ([guide](#love-at-the-right-time))

**Q239: (b)** Consistent household structure and boundaries — not unlimited comfort that blurs rank and thresholds. Separation stress improves with structure at home and earned access — not indulgence that deepens dependency. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q240: (b)** Stick assist — leash to a short stick on the ground for a consistent downward jerk without upward tension. Small dogs still need calibrated correction. The stick assist makes a downward jerk achievable and consistent. ([guide](#guide-training--leash))

**Q241: (c)** The same rank test is physically unmanageable at full size — thresholds are safety equipment now. Giant breeds make doorway and body-space rules critical early. Cute leaning becomes dangerous mass — you set thresholds now. ([guide](#guide-leadership--front-door))

**Q242: (b)** Reward earned calm after structured reset — comforting during the episode often feeds the loop. Elevated stress sensitivity plus in-moment soothing can spiral. Structure and timing matter more than emotional rescue. ([guide](#love-at-the-right-time))

**Q243: (b)** Same standard, calibrated delivery — indulgence spirals are especially common at toy scale. High stress sensitivity is not permission to skip structure. Small indulgence pitfalls intensify at toy scale. ([guide](#common-pitfalls-the-human-baby-trap))

**Q244: (d)** Structured outlets and handler-led work — idle drive becomes rehearsal without a job frame. High-drive types need job-like structure. Without it they self-assign work that rehearses unwanted patterns — you lead the job. ([guide](#guide-training--access))

**Q245: (a)** Deliver calm matter-of-fact correction, then rebuild warmth — structure without affection reads as abandonment. Clingy breeds need fair correction with a quick rebuild. Cold withdrawal or avoiding standards damages these dogs. ([guide](#breed-temperament-universal-principles-flexible-application))

**Q246: (c)** Attention demand — withhold engagement until calm; do not reward the paw cycle. Forceful pawing is demand for a dopamine hit, not affection. Become a rock — look away until the body settles. ([guide](#symptom-glossary))

**Q247: (b)** Pack guarding instinct — protecting a vulnerable pack member, not pure annoyance. Elimination leaves an animal vulnerable; pack-guard behaviour reframes resentment. Thresholds still apply in training mode. ([guide](#pack-guarding-the-bathroom-follow))

**Q248: (b)** At this mass you cannot out-muscle a committed lunge — engaged core and stance are safety, not polish. Raw mass at 40–50+ kg makes your body mechanics a safety requirement — you cannot negotiate after he commits. ([guide](#handling-and-physical-mechanics))

**Q249: (a)** Puppy mindset in you must end — project certainty; the standard starts at the door, not on the walk. At two years many large dogs are in physical prime. Handler clarity and door standards are how he learns adulthood. ([guide](#leadership-through-clarity))

**Q250: (c)** At the threshold before permission — eye contact and calm body verified before the door opens. The standard starts at the front door. Permission before action — not correction only after he is already out. ([guide](#leadership-through-clarity))

**Q251: (d)** Recall failure is not a game — pursue joylessly and relentlessly without drama he can feed on. Ignoring recall cannot be treated as minor. Pursue without tension — the message is that running away cannot win. ([guide](#recall-leash-culture-and-road-safety))

**Q252: (a)** After calm coordination and focus are shown — access to runs and sniffs is your reward, not his demand. Biological outlets happen on your terms. He earns runs and sniffs through calm structure first — not by escalating pressure. ([guide](#biological-needs--on-your-terms))

**Q253: (d)** Keep structure — leash, space, and earned calm before close contact; do not assume the other handler will manage. Unstructured meetings with unfamiliar intact dogs are not worth the gamble. Control space and contact until calm is earned. ([guide](#first-meetings-and-earned-freedom))

**Q254: (a)** At the precursor — before the body fully commits; break visual lock and redirect while you still have leverage. Read the ready stance early — at this mass a late correction is a handler emergency. Intervene before he commits. ([guide](#handling-and-physical-mechanics))

**Q255: (b)** Removing testosterone can worsen baseline fear-reactivity or shyness rather than fixing it. Testosterone is described as a crucial stabilizer for some anxious dogs in this model. Neutering can worsen baseline fear-reactivity. ([guide](#the-physical-baseline-health-vs-hormones))
